#7862. Let’s Be SMART – Successfully Managing Animal Rights Today

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

Letâs Be S.M.A.R.T. in Keratea, Greece, is a truly unique organization, currently home to over 100 cats and 13 dogs, living in a cage-free, home-like, villa-style environment. S.M.A.R.T. stands for Successfully Managing Animal Rights Today, and for Julie Kelley, founder and manager of this international animal welfare organization, that means working towards global animal welfare, sharing essential information and facts about animals worldwide, and helping people understand the benefits that come from treating animals with compassion and care.

I had been traveling to Greece since 1998 and would see the issues with stray cats and dogs.  I felt very comfortable in Greece. I had business with Greek nationals in New York, learned a lot of the language, and understood the cultural differences. I felt it was my mission to create Letâs Be S.M.A.R.T. to help people understand the great benefits animals provide to us humans and to educate young people as well. Of course, after a couple of years, it was hard not to take in the first kitty who gave birth, and well, it just grew exponentially from there! Since 2007, we have added many programs and special projects to continue our quest to provide the best we can for our strays.

Letâs be S.M.A.R.T. aims to educate the public about the importance of animals by raising awareness of their rights, well-being, and care. We believe in thinking globally and acting locally by supporting special projects as they arise and, through our programs, bringing communities together to promote responsible animal care.

In Greece, our campaign is primarily centred on reducing the suffering, abuse, and neglect of animals while increasing public awareness of their needs and rights. These include running an innovative and modern foster home, managing a rehoming program for rescued animals, and collaborating with municipalities to implement effective stray animal care initiatives. We also provide practical solutions for supporting strays in urban communitiesâsuch as ensuring access to food and waterâand we actively engage philanthropic individuals who travel to Greece to volunteer, learn about shelter medicine, and receive training in best practices in animal care.

The creation of the sanctuary and setting up the organization in Greece was a huge accomplishment. Let's be S.M.A.R.T. is always evolving with fresh ideas to make life better for the cats and dogs we have in our care.

Our campaign model is unique in Greece. We have created the âSMART Starfish approachâ in which all five arms must function together to create the best outcome.

Each arm of the starfish represents a core pillar of our mission:

Sterilization â controlling population growth at its source

Medical Care & Microchipping â restoring health and identity

Feeding & Shelter â stability, nourishment, and safety

Education & Community â knowledge that shapes future behavior

NGO Collaboration â collective strength through partnership

For years, our programs and ideas have been influencing how animal charities operate and making permanent changes for a better future for animal welfare in Greece.

We created the following programs: Volunteer, SMART Family Video Series, Veterinary Internship, SMART Yards, and Adoption Vacation, all of which are operational every day and are detailed on the Programs page on our website, if you would like to take a closer look. We could not function without the help of our amazing Volunteers.

We successfully found wonderful homes for 73 cats in 2025. I'm not 100% sure, but I would say we are one of the leading cat adopters in Greece!

We receive multiple enquiries from tourists who have found a cat or kitten, and they want to take it home with them to their country. Many times they have cared for them during their stay, provided medicine, bottle-fed babies, etc. This has become increasingly common, with visitors seeing cats all over Greece. Therefore, I decided to offer the Adoption-Vacation as a package. We care for the kitten or cat until it is ready to travel, taking care of the necessary vaccines, passport, microchip, etc. Once the cat is ready to travel, we make travel arrangements with the adopter.

You can see our cats, kittens, and dogs for adoption on our website and have a video chat with us about your requirements and meet a cat if you have already fallen in love (we created a Kitty Picker to help you choose the character of your cat), and then arrange a visit with us when you arrive in Greece. If the home check is secured, we arrange the papers for your new pet to travel home with you. Or we can foster a cat you rescue while you are in Greece and deal with the veterinary needs, papers etc. The cat can travel after you leave with a flight buddy or one of our volunteers.

What better souvenir to have from Greece than a beautiful cat that needed special love and care?

Everything we do is linked. The more sterilizations we achieve, the safer and healthier the animals are in the community; they are interacting better with each other, and people know they are sterilized.

We would like the municipalities and communities all over Greece to enjoy the benefits of the SMART Yards and help take care of the animals. Working together is the future.  We are also collaborating with some officials regarding some policies involving the strays and to help create some standards for housing the strays. Animals and people need to coexist in a humane way. Not every cat needs to be inside a home but can remain cared for and part of our ecosystem.

A rather big goal is to find someone to help us purchase the property we rent, make refurbishments and sustainable features, and add a vet clinic for shared use with other charities and our vet interns. This is a tall order, but we are looking for someone who would like to leave a legacy.

We also want to extend our ability to provide food and shelter after sterilization so that every animal is cared for.

Our animals live in a home-style environment, so every day is the same as if they were living in a family home. Cats are either in bedrooms; we have a retirement room, a special dietary needs room, and a kitten nursery, each with cats that are selected to share a room together, or they are in the main house and free to mingle and hang out on our netted balconies in cute wooden houses and take in the fresh air and nature, since we are in a rural setting, just 15 minutes from Athens International Airport.

Some of the funniest moments are with kittens and playful cats. Plus, bonded pairs â we have a husband-and-wife team called Jasper and Margot who need to be adopted together, and they are very entertaining with their games and spats.

Cats and dogs choose who they like and want to go home with. We find people fall in love with cats that come to them, and a chemistry is formed. Sometimes a visitor leaves, and they cannot stop thinking about the cat they fell in love with and make an application to adopt. We are so happy when this happens. We have repeat adoptions from families and visitors all over the world. We also have Sponsors and Patreon for people to support our work.

Volunteering is open to everyone around the world who would like to come to stay and help us. If you love animals, it's an opportunity to help save lives. It's pure joy to see a cat or dog that was sick transform into good health and finally live in a wonderful family home. That's what the team at Let's be S.M.A.R.T. wants for them all: to be safe, healthy, and happy.

People can also help by following, subscribing, and sharing us on socials. Donations are greatly appreciated, as are supplies, and we created the Amazon Wishlist so gifts can be sent to us directly from Amazon Germany, tax-free.

If youâre visiting Greece and see a lot of stray cats, itâs a good idea to ask around if there is a local organization helping to take care of them. If you see an injured cat, you should immediately try to find a responsible person or contact the local police.

You can also post on local social media groups to try to find help. Most of the cats we take into our foster home settings are from tourists or residents who find our website through a Google search. It is hard to avoid helping, but I would suggest not removing an animal from their setting to a hotel room or Airbnb, and then leaving and putting it back on the street. The cat can get disoriented and perhaps be in danger.

We truly hope to have more controlled community care for our strays in the future.

Plenty of garden pests spend winter as eggs or dormant adults in old vines, twigs, and leaves. Remove them during fall cleanup – but spare the helpful insects.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

By late October, the vegetable beds are mostly dead vines, and the shrubs are dropping leaves. At that point, fall cleanup is usually just tidying up. Next year's garden pests are still in that mess, though. Squash bugs shelter under the old vines, moths leave egg masses on bark and lawn chairs, and beetles seal their eggs inside viburnum twigs.

Many common garden pests don't die off in winter. They spend it as eggs, pupae, or dormant adults in one spot, and they mostly stay there until spring. That makes them pretty easy to find and remove right now. A pair of pruners, a putty knife, or a rake can take out a whole tent caterpillar colony before it ever hatches.

Where you look depends on the pest. Some hide their eggs inside twigs, while others leave them right out on bark or a fence post. A few of the egg cases and cocoons you'll find belong to beneficial insects, though, and those should stay put.

Insects that overwinter usually ride out the cold in a resting stage. For a lot of garden pests, that means an egg mass on a twig, a pupa in the soil, or an adult wedged under leaf litter. Eggs and pupae can't scatter, and dormant adults barely move. Bare branches help too – egg masses hidden by summer foliage are much easier to spot once the leaves fall. One scraped egg mass in October can mean hundreds fewer caterpillars in spring.

So why not rake up everything? Good insects spend the winter in the same spots as the bad ones. Lady beetles and ground beetles burrow into leaf litter, and many native bees tuck into hollow stems. Strip every bed bare during fall cleanup, and those go, too. Focus on whatever had problems this year, and leave the rest a little messy.

Here's where some common pests spend the winter and how to clear them out.

Squash bugs (Anasa tristis) are still around after the plants die. Adults crawl under dead vines and leaf litter for the winter, and some hide under nearby boards. Clear that out once the squash and pumpkins are done. Those vines are prickly, so you'll need good protective gloves like these nitrile-coated garden gloves from Home Depot. Bag the vines rather than piling them up, or the bugs move right in.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

If your viburnums got chewed up this summer, the leaf beetles (Pyrrhalta viburni) probably left eggs in the twigs. You won't see the eggs, just little rows of bumps near the tips of this year's branches once the leaves are off. Those are the caps the females made from chewed bark. Cut the twigs off with sharp bypass pruning shears (these Fiskars bypass pruners on Amazon are good value for money if you need a new pair) and trash them before spring.

Eastern tent caterpillars (Malacosoma americanum) mostly feed on cherry and apple trees, so start there. Look along the thin twigs for a shiny black band, like someone dripped varnish around the branch. That's the egg mass. Snip the twig off or crush the band, and throw it out. For a big tree, Monterey horticultural oil works as a late-winter dormant spray that can smother the eggs.

Anyone in the Northeast or upper Midwest has likely heard of spongy moth (Lymantria dispar), once called gypsy moth. Its caterpillars can strip a tree bare in a bad year. Right now, though, they're just eggs, packed by the hundreds into tan, fuzzy patches on tree trunks and fences. Check sheds and the underside of patio chairs, too. Scrape each patch into a bucket of soapy water – a soft-sided tub like this Tubtrugs one from Walmart works well – and let it soak for several days.

Iris borer moths (Macronoctua onusta) lay their eggs on old iris leaves in late summer and early fall, and the eggs wait there until spring. Then the caterpillars hatch, climb the new leaves, and tunnel down into the rhizome. Wait until after a hard frost, since the moths can keep laying until then, and cut away the old leaves. Dispose of the foliage in the trash rather than adding it to your compost pile.

If you've had trouble with iris borers before, consider keeping a spinosad-based insecticide, such as Bonide Captain Jack's Deadbug Brew, on hand for spring, when newly hatched caterpillars are vulnerable to treatment before they burrow into the rhizomes.

Scale insects (Coccoidea) stay stuck to the stems and branches of shrubs and trees all winter. They look like small bumps that come off with a scrape of a fingernail. It could be an adult female, a young one, or a cover with eggs under it, depending on the type of scale. Scrub off what you can, and treat the tiny crawlers with Garden Safe insecticidal soap, available on Amazon. Look over potted citrus before bringing it inside, since scale can keep breeding indoors.

Plenty of aphids (Aphididae) get through winter as eggs on rose canes and fruit tree twigs, especially on apples. Those eggs are tiny, black, and shiny, and they're usually near a bud or in a crack in the bark. They're hard to see without a 10x handheld magnifier, like this one with a built-in light on Amazon. Winter pruning gets rid of many, and a dormant oil spray before the buds start to swell can kill more. If some still hatch, a spray of Bonide neem oil from Walmart can help.

Lady beetles, lacewings, mantises, butterflies, and native bees overwinter in the garden too. Don't remove these beneficial insects.

Lady beetles tend to bunch up in winter, and raking into the leaves at the base of a tree can turn up a whole cluster. Cover them back up and move on. Both adults and larvae eat aphids, and every beetle that survives the winter is one more working the garden next year.

Mantis egg cases look like dried globs of tan foam, sometimes as big as a golf ball, glued to a stem or twig. If one is on a stem, you need to cut below the case and tuck the stem into a shrub, off the ground. Mantises do eat helpful insects, too.

Lacewing eggs are easy to recognize – each one perches on the tip of a hair-thin silk stalk. By fall, you're more likely to find the round, papery cocoons that larvae spin in hidden spots on plants, or adults sheltering in leaf litter. The larvae are voracious aphid predators. Leave both stages in place.

Black swallowtail caterpillars spend the summer eating parsley and dill, and the last ones of the year don't leave in fall – they hang on through winter as brown chrysalises, sometimes on the old herb stems. One looks a lot like a scrap of dead plant, so go slowly when you cut those herbs back.

Native bees need a winter spot, too. Many of them nest in the ground, and bare soil is easier to dig into than mulch. Leave a patch or two uncovered. Other bees use hollow or pithy stems like raspberry canes, and their young spend the winter sealed inside. Leave those stems standing until spring warms up, then cut them back to about knee height.

A clean garden and a healthy garden aren't always the same thing. Cut the marked twigs, scrape the egg masses, and clear out the old squash vines and iris leaves. Then let the rest of the leaves lie. Next spring should bring fewer squash bugs and more lady beetles.

Tyler’s passion began with indoor gardening and deepened as he studied plant-fungi interactions in controlled settings. With a microbiology background focused on fungi, he’s spent over a decade solving tough and intricate gardening problems. After spinal injuries and brain surgery, Tyler’s approach to gardening changed. It became less about the hobby and more about recovery and adapting to physical limits. His growing success shows that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.

Keeping a bird bath ice-free could mean life or death for your garden birds this winter.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

As we head further into fall, it’s time to take steps to stop a bird bath freezing over and depriving birds of this valuable resource. Birds need daily access to water and when natural sources freeze over, a bird bath can become a vital lifeline and bring feathered friends flocking to your yard. During a cold snap, dehydration kills birds far faster than starvation, so keeping an ice-free bird bath this winter really is a lifesaver.

Water is surprisingly necessary to so many elements of avian survival in winter, and most small garden birds must drink at least once a day simply to stay alive. As insects become scarce as temperatures fall, a diet consisting primarily of seeds and nuts means birds need to drink more to digest their food, and in sub-zero conditions, eating snow isn’t an option for small birds because of their limited body heat.

A reliable water source also enables birds to bathe and preen, zipping individual feather barbs back together daily to maintain a waterproof insulating top layer. Vital to trap body heat on cold nights, this is also essential for efficient flight – and bare winter branches can leave birds vulnerable to predators. Keep your bird bath unfrozen and you’ll also help birds preserve energy they would otherwise waste finding an alternative water source. So, whether yours is a simple DIY bird bath you made yourself or the smartest birdie bowl money can buy, here's how to stop the water freezing over.

Seems obvious, right? But while the best place for a bird bath in summer is in partial shade to prevent algae growth, a sunnier spot in winter will help to keep a bird bath ice-free. Remember that the sunniest winter spot in your garden may be different to where the sunshine hits in summer, because the sun is lower in the sky. Think about prevailing wind direction, too, as a breeze will increase heat loss from any liquid, just as you blow on your cup of coffee to cool it down, and speed the freezing process in cold conditions.

Positioning your bird bath around 6 feet from a south-facing wall is an optimum solution. Not only will the water be warmed by sunshine for most of the day, the wall will shelter the bath from cold northerly winds and also act as a solar radiator, reflecting the sun’s heat or absorbing then releasing it once the air temperature cools. Either way, your bird bath will sit in a microclimate and the water will be slower to freeze and quicker to thaw.

Solar power is also the force behind this idea as dark stones will absorb the sun’s heat during the day, then release it as the air cools, to slow or stop bird baths freezing over. To be effective, the rock needs to be at least 4 inches across, but do match it to the size of the bird bath as it shouldn’t displace more than a third of the water. The stone should protrude above the water line as an exposed surface will heat far more quickly than a submerged one. The darker and denser the rock, the more heat it will hold, and a flattish surface will absorb more warmth.

Any object that floats on the surface of the water will constantly disrupt ice crystal formation, so it takes longer for the bird bath to freeze. Tailor your choice of what to float to how exposed your garden is, as the object needs to be light enough to move on the slightest of breezes but heavy enough to stay put in stronger winds.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

In a sheltered corner, a ping pong ball is best; in a windy position, try a tennis ball. But in most gardens adding a rubber duck to your bird bath hits the sweet spot, and it doesn’t have to be yellow as this Mallard Rubber Duck from Amazon shows.

To reliably prevent ice in bird baths, use a de-icer, but be smart when shopping as many products sold as bird bath de-icers were designed for chicken coops. Look for a product with a thermostat that only works when temperatures drop and automatically shuts off once the weather warms up, so it uses minimal energy. You only need to prevent the water from freezing, not keep it warm, so a product that’s rated 60-120 watts is ideal; leave those 1000W designs for the chickens!

Another important consideration is the length of the lead, as birds often won’t use a bath positioned too close to a wall. Think about the size of your bath, too. This 9” Thermostatic Birdbath Heater from Amazon with a 5.9’ cord is great for a bigger bird bath, while this smaller 100W Bird Bath Heater, also from Amazon, with a 5’ cord would be better for an average-sized bath.

If garden aesthetics are important to you, then faux-rock designs such as this 60W Bird Bath DeIcer from Walmart bring a more natural look. You can also buy heated birdbaths with options to fit onto deck posts and balcony rails as well as ground stakes.

As temperatures drop and natural water sources freeze over, your ice-free bird bath will become a magnet for neighborhood birds. All that splashing avian action will mean you’ll need to keep the bath topped up as the bigger the volume of water, the more stable its temperature. Clear out any fallen leaves, too, as tannins will leach out and make the water unpalatable and rotting plant matter will invite unwelcome bacteria into your birdy spa.

It’s vital to scrub your bird bath once a week, particularly if neighbors don’t bother to keep their bird baths ice-free and yours becomes very busy, as that higher traffic means disease spreads more easily between birds. Use a bird-safe cleaner such as Bird Saver, available from Walmart, or a dilute solution of 10% vinegar and a scrubbing brush, and rinse well before refilling with water.

All these simple ways will keep a water supply for your garden birds, and bring feathered friends flocking to your yard through winter. So, if you're switching up your bird-feeding routine for colder weather, whether that's putting up an extra feeder, adding seasonal kitchen treats or planting shrubs laden with winter berries that birds adore, it's essential to take steps to ensure there's water alongside that welcome food.

#7859. When Art Meets Animal Rescue: A Creative Way to Help Dogs Find Homes

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

We often turn to art for pleasure, curiosity, or a feeling we canât quite put into words. A painting catches our attention; a sculpture makes us pause. But art inspiring us to adopt a dog? Now thereâs a plot twist.

The Rescue Collection is an exciting project created through a collaboration between The Sato Project, creative agencies BLKJ Havas Singapore and Havas New York, and Brooklynâs Powerhouse Arts. The program brings adoptable dogs into the art gallery and uses observations of their responses to create individual artistic profiles. The aim is to help potential adopters see the dogs beyond their appearance, breed, or uncertain past.

Itâs an unusual approach to a familiar challenge: helping rescue dogs get noticed in a crowded adoption landscape.

At Powerhouse Arts in Brooklyn, animal welfare scientist Dr. Holly Molinaro observed dogs from The Sato Project as they explored different artworks. The dogs first had time to sniff around and become comfortable in the unfamiliar space. Their responses were then observed, including whether they looked at, sniffed, or moved away from particular pieces, or chose to lie down nearby.

Rudolph, for example, chose to lie down in front of some sculptures but ignored others. These observations helped shape profiles associating the dogs with artistic styles such as Surrealism, Minimalism, Figurative art, and Abstraction.

The concept is playful, but its purpose is practical. A standard adoption photograph may show what a dog looks like; a creative profile offers another reason to stop scrolling and learn more about the animal behind the image.

Someone might come for the art and leave wanting a dog. Turns out, the best thing in the gallery might have four legs and be up for adoption.

The Sato Project rescues dogs in Puerto Rico and helps place them in homes, including in the northeastern United States. Some arrive with limited information about their histories, and assumptions about a dogâs background can influence how potential adopters perceive them.

A dogâs history can help rescue teams understand what support an animal may need and how to approach introductions to a new home. But the past doesnât tell the whole story. A complicated backstory might tell us where a dog has been. It doesnât tell us everything about who they are. Dogs, much like people, are so much more than their basic profile.

Dogs respond to the world as individuals. One may eagerly approach a stranger, while another prefers to observe from a safe distance. Neither reaction alone defines the dogâs personality or tells us what kind of companion they might become with time and appropriate support.

The Rescue Collection offers a different starting point. Instead of focusing on what is known about a dogâs past, it invites people to become curious about the dog in front of them. That first spark of interest can matter, especially for dogs who might otherwise be overlooked.

Dogs explore their surroundings through several senses, and their behavior around unfamiliar objects can offer clues about what attracts their attention. But interpreting those responses requires care.

Dogs also see color differently from humans. People typically have three types of color-sensitive cone cells in their retinas, while dogs have two, a form of vision known as dichromacy. Dogs distinguish blues and yellows relatively well but have more difficulty differentiating reds and greens. Their visual experience of the world is therefore different from ours.

That doesnât mean dogs see the world in black and white. Color is only one possible influence on how they respond to an object. Shape, contrast, texture, scent, movement, and the surrounding environment may also play a part.

Nor does spending longer near a sculpture necessarily mean a dog prefers its artistic style. The dog may be interested in its shape or position, or simply feel comfortable resting there.

A single gallery visit cannot establish an animalâs overall personality or predict how they will behave around children, other dogs, or visitors at home. Behavior is best understood across time and situations.

A sculpture might have us admiring its color and form. The dog? They might be more interested in giving it a sniff. Different critics, different criteria.

Although the profiles are not scientific personality assessments or guarantees of compatibility, they do invite us to learn more about each dog. Conversations with the rescue team and time spent meeting the dog remain essential to finding a suitable match.

Rescue work involves far more than finding adopters. Veterinary care, foster placements, transportation, behavioral support, and follow-up all require time and resources. Helping the public connect with the dogs is only one part of that work, but an important one.

The Sato Projectâs adoption and foster manager, Alessandra Migliore, said the organization was excited to explore new ways of showcasing its dogsâ personalities. The campaign is part of the organizationâs broader work to help dogs rescued in Puerto Rico find homes in the northeastern United States.

A creative campaign cannot guarantee adoption, and an appealing profile is only the beginning. But an unexpected introduction may reach someone who wasnât actively looking for a dog, or encourage a prospective adopter to look beyond their first impressions.

The Rescue Collection hopes to help more rescue dogs connect with potential adopters. Its message says it best: âSee the masterpiece inside every dog.â

Art might catch someoneâs eye, but getting to know the dog is what matters. And if a sculpture-loving visitor leaves the gallery thinking about adoption, thatâs a pretty good review.

Explore The Rescue Collection, use its rescue-finding tool to search by city or postcode, or meet dogs waiting for homes through The Sato Project.

Automatic litter boxes are not just a serious time saver for cat owners; theyâre also hugely beneficial for cats, particularly those that refuse to use anything but a fresh bed of cat litter. Yet, some cat parents are hesitant about the idea of bringing home a self-cleaning litter box.

In my experience, there are two big reasons cat parents hesitate to make the switch from a traditional litter pan to a fancy self-cleaning litter box.

The first reason is all about the cat. Many owners fear that their cat wonât be able to adjust to the design of an automatic litter box. While traditional tray boxes are wide open on top and allow plenty of room for big cats to turn around, dig, and stand tall as they do their business, most automatic boxes are more compact.

The second issue that keeps many parents scooping manually rather than investing in a box that can do it for them is about safety.

Automatic litter boxes have a lot of moving parts. Many turn completely upside down while cleaning, so itâs natural to be worried that your cat could be frightened, pinched, or trapped by the mechanism. Of course, these boxes have

sensors and safety controls to minimize the risks of an accident, but no technology is foolproof.

With their new automatic litter box, Neakasa listened to the most common concerns of hesitant cat parents and used them to inspire their design.

For the big or claustrophobic kitty, the M9 offers a wide-open, spacious design. The bowl-shaped hood isnât as open as a traditional pan without a roof, but the tilted angle and wide mouth make it much easier for large cats to navigate. And plenty of headspace means even big kitties like Maine Coons and Ragdolls can stand up tall while they do their business.

For the claustrophobic kitty, the M9 has another trick up its sleeve: the hood and âcabinâ of the litter box are translucent. This means plenty of light gets inside, and your cat has the ability to see all around them while they assume that oh-so vulnerable position.

The Neakasa M9 Automatic Litter Box also has plenty of reassuring features for even the most nervous owner.

This box has many of the same safety sensors that most other automatic boxes do. These work to prevent cleaning while the cat is present and stop cleaning if your cat leaps inside mid-cycle. But what makes the M9 different is that it is structurally designed to be safe even if those sensors fail.

Thanks to the spherical design and âtilt-safeâ rotation, even if the box were to somehow enter cleaning mode while your cat was inside, they would just get a bit of a ride (like a kitty in a hamster ball). Because the M9 cabin is free of pinch points and the opening does not close or shrink during cleaning, it would be virtually impossible for a cat to be harmed.

This is exactly the kind of fail-safe design nervous cat parents need.

Founded in 2017 as Neabot, Neakasa is a smart home and pet-care technology brand headquartered in Shenzhen, China, with offices in Los Angeles and Tokyo.

Its products aim to simplify everyday cleaning and pet care. Beyond automatic litter boxes, Neakasa offers pet grooming kits with vacuum technology, smart pet water fountains, and even air-purifying litter box steps.

As you can guess, the Neakasa M9 Automatic Litter Box is a great option for larger kitties and those who arenât likely to enjoy the cramped quarters of traditional automatic litter boxes. Itâs also great for safety-conscious owners.

My 12-pound Domestic Shorthair, Makoa, and I have tested a lot of automatic litter boxes in our time, and I can say with all honesty that the M9 from Neakasa is a true standout.

The litter box arrived in a rather large box with a somewhat overwhelming number of parts. But I promise you that it looks much harder than it is to put this together. Following the quick installation guide, I had it up and ready to go in less than ten minutes.

Insider tip: The installation instructions donât mention that the orange fixing ring (waste guide) at the back of the cabin must first be removed before the cabin can fit into the base.

I did have a bit of a problem getting the litter box to connect to my WiFi, which was interesting because I recently tested the Neakasa Riko Automatic Cat Feeder in the same room, using the same app, and had zero issues. But this could have just been an anomaly, because the next day I tried again and it connected right away.

Once the app was connected, everything was straightforward to set up. From there, it was hands-offâand Makoaâs time to test.

I set the M9 up in the laundry room next to his current automatic cat box, which is a more typical robot cat box with an enclosed cabin and full roof design. Anytime he has a traditional litter pan available, he will always choose that over his current automatic litter box.

The step up into the M9 is a bit high. For smaller cats or those with mobility problems, I recommend checking out the Neakasa Air Step. I have one of these and ended up putting it in front of the M9 to catch litter, but Makoa definitely liked using it as a step as well.

In terms of odor control, cleaning prowess, and ease of use, this litter box performed exceptionally well.  As expected, the cleaning cycle stops if it senses weight or movement in the cabin, but I still really appreciate the smart design that makes it virtually impossible for a cat to get pinched or trapped if the safety sensors somehow failed and the cleaning cycle started while they were inside.

Overall, I have been really happy with this litter box, both in terms of its design and how well it cleans and reduces odors. More importantly, Makoa loves the larger space and open feel.

The 6-liter waste bin is advertised to last approximately 7â10 days for one cat, which I found to be pretty accurate. Households with multiple cats will likely need to empty it more frequently.

#7855. Is That Really A Service Dog?

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

For years, business owners and property managers have wrestled with the same question: how do you tell the difference between a legitimate service animal and a pet that someone is trying to pass off as one?

Itâs a question John Bradford spent years trying to answer, first as a property manager overseeing thousands of rental units, and now as the founder of PetScreening, a platform used to verify animal accommodation requests across more than 7 million rental units nationwide.

With the rising number of service dogs and emotional support animals leading to incidents of confusion, conflict, and exploitation, John sets the record straight on how to verify a real service animal from one that isn't, and what you are legally allowed to ask.

The truth is that most people donât fully understand the laws around service animals and emotional support animals, and even well-meaning questions can come across as anything but. That gray area and confusion can create real risk. Ask the wrong question, and a business can face a discrimination complaint. Ask no questions at all, and policies and rules become easy to bend, which leads to potentially dangerous situations.

Getting this right protects everyone involved, including the people who genuinely rely on these animals every day.

Under the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), service animals are defined as:

âDogs that are individually trained to do work or perform tasks for people with disabilities.â

Disabilities vary widely, from physical and sensory to psychiatric, intellectual, and neurological. The needs of each person are different, so the trained tasks may look different from person to person.  The ADA cites that the service animal must be a dog or, in rare cases, a miniature horse. Federal law does not require certifications, registrations, vests, or ID cards for these animals.

Beyond the specification that the animal must be trained to perform tasks, the legal standard is limited, so it can be difficult to easily identify which animals are legitimately service dogs and which are not. This is where public confusion starts.

There are plenty of ways to make a dog look like a service animal, like labeled vests, âregistrationâ certifications, and IDs, but none of these are federally supported. A dog wearing a vest isnât automatically a service animal, and a dog without one isnât automatically a pet. What matters legally is not appearance or paperwork. Itâs the dogâs trained ability to perform certain tasks.

This is the distinction many find hardest to grasp, and it matters because different laws apply to each. Service dogs are protected under the ADA and, due to their training and the tasks they perform, they are permitted in public spaces such as restaurants, retail stores, and hotels. That could mean guiding someone who is visually impaired, alerting an owner to an oncoming seizure, or reminding them to take medication. Service animals are also protected under the Fair Housing Act and require paperwork if the disability or need for the animal is not obviously understood.

Emotional support animals (ESAs) are different. Their value comes from the comfort their presence provides. They donât necessarily have to be dogs, they arenât required to be trained to perform specific tasks, and theyâre not covered by the ADA to be allowed in public spaces like restaurants.

They are, however, protected by the Fair Housing Act. Under this, landlords are generally required to make allowances for an ESA if a tenant has appropriate documentation from a licensed healthcare provider establishing a disability-related need. Examples of disabilities warranting an ESA include, but are not limited to, anxiety disorders or autism.

ESA accommodations are supposed to come through legitimate means, typically an established relationship with a licensed medical or mental health professional who can document the need. But some people have found loopholes for this by filling out forms online or paying fees for instant letters, which only fuels public skepticism about the legitimate need for these animals. Not to mention, this abuse can make people wary of service dogs, too.

While there is no foolproof visual test, trained service animals typically display consistent, recognizable behaviors. These dogs show exemplary discipline and obedience to the commands of their handler. They have the ability to ignore external distractions from other dogs, people, food, sounds, and smells while focusing on the needs of their handler. They display a calm temperament and are not aggressive or anxious. It is also expected that these animals be quiet, unless they are tasked with alerting an owner to a medical issue, and that they are housebroken and trained to walk on a leash without unnecessary pulling or circling.

This is where business owners and landlords need to tread carefully. When it isnât obvious that a dog is a service animal, staff are permitted to ask:

Is this dog required because of a disability?

What task has it been trained to perform?

Thatâs the full extent of it. Staff should not ask about the nature of a personâs disability, demand documentation or proof of training, or require dogs to demonstrate their tasks. Asking beyond the two questions, even if it comes from a place of genuine curiosity or caution, can expose a business to discrimination claims.

News stories about supposed service animals harming bystanders in public continue to raise questions about the legitimacy of those animals, and businesses are often caught in the crossfire. These incidents are symptoms of a larger problem: businesses and property owners navigating without clear guidance, while people with legitimate needs are met with suspicion.

Service animals and emotional support animals play an essential role in the lives of the people who rely on them, and protecting that role starts with understanding the rules.

If you own a business or manage a property, you donât need to become legal experts overnight, but you do need a consistent, fair process that respects peopleâs rights and keeps everyone safe. When everyone knows where the lines are, the people who truly depend on these animals can go about their lives without facing doubt at every door.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In late fall, bird feeders start emptying a lot faster. Black-capped chickadees make trip after trip to cache seeds in tree bark, while northern cardinals arrive at the crack of dawn and linger until dusk. As fall nights lengthen and temperatures plunge, small songbirds burn through a lot of stored body fat just to get through a long, cold night and maintain core body temperatures of 105°F (40°C) until sunrise.

Summer's bugs are mostly gone, and whatever is left on the coneflowers and dogwoods will be getting rapidly picked over as the weeks go by. So your local birds need all the help they can get. But you don't have to buy anything special or massively expensive to start feeding birds this time of year. Key kitchen scraps set out alongside the seed can give them a little extra boost in the next few weeks. Even a bruised apple or a few plain peanuts can help to keep them going.

Transforming a few everyday, wholesome kitchen leftovers into supplemental treats provides immediate, calorie-dense relief right when birds need it most. However, it’s important to be discerning and use the right scraps. Birds possess delicate digestive systems. Salty or moldy leftovers can make a bird sick, and a couple of common kitchen foods are toxic to them. So make sure you are topping up your feeding supplies with the right handy kitchen scraps – to help out hungry beaks on a budget.

If you’re offering your birdie pals these “cheep and cheerful” kitchen scraps (pun intended), just be mindful of cleanliness and portion control. Fresh scraps lack the protective husks of wild seeds, so they spoil rapidly when exposed to fall damp. Leftovers that sit out overnight can sour, harbor harmful bacteria, or attract nocturnal scavengers such as rats. Offer only modest quantities in the morning which birds will devour by early afternoon, and sweep away any uneaten remnants before dusk.

Keeping things clean is critical, as communal feeding areas can easily become hotspots for infections. Feeding trays and platform feeders need a scrub every week or so, and sooner after rain or heavy traffic. Soak feeder elements in 1 part bleach to 9 parts water, then rinse and let them dry before refilling them. If you’re using a tube feeder, it’s worth investing in a long brush like the Songbird Essentials Extra Long Bottle Brush, available from Amazon, for a versatile bargain to speed up cleaning.

And don’t forget to keep your fresh water supplies regularly topped up in tandem with these kitchen scraps. Birds require plenty of clean drinking water to metabolize high-calorie foods, as well as bathing water to clean their feathers. As night frosts become frequent, it’s a good idea to install a birdbath de-icer or a heated bird bath, such as the Allied Precision Heated Bird Bath with Mounted Bracket, also from Amazon, to protect your water.

Have fun watching your birds pick over these scraps. They aren’t intended to replace your regular bird feeds. But they can give some delightful added nourishment during these trickier transitional weeks. So put some of these out, a little at a time, and enjoy the birdlife putting the following leftovers to good use in these chilly fall mornings.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Those soft, bruised apples and pears lingering at the bottom of the fruit bowl make yummy supplemental treats for backyard birds. These sweet pomes deliver quick, easily digestible carbs and sugars, not to mention vital moisture. Fruit-eating species such as American robins, northern mockingbirds, eastern bluebirds, gray catbirds, and nomadic cedar waxwings will eagerly feast on fresh diced fruit.

Preparation is key: always cut apples and pears into small, bite-sized cubes (roughly a quarter-inch) to make them manageable for smaller bills. Make sure you remove all the seeds (or pips) out of the cores. Apple seeds contain a compound that can release cyanide. And any moldy pieces need to go in the compost. Fruit-eaters rarely visit seed tubes, so set the pieces on a sturdy, open platform feeder like the Kingsyard Platform Feeder from Amazon, which can house a healthy bird feast in comfort and safety.

When clearing out the pantry, there are usually some dry rolled oats or steel-cut oats sitting at the bottom of a canister. This can make a wholesome carbo boost for birdies. Uncooked oats supply fiber, minerals, and steady energy for ground-foraging birds. Mourning doves, dark-eyed juncos, song sparrows, and native towhees will all happily hoover up any scattered across a low ground tray or gravel border.

Just make sure they are raw, plain, and dry. Never set out leftover cooked oatmeal, as cooked porridge turns into a gummy paste. Furthermore, steer clear of instant flavored oat packets, which are loaded with refined sugars, salt, and artificial flavorings. Scatter only a handful at a time on dry days, as wet oats quickly sour and congeal. And make sure to supplement your oats with a hearty wild bird mix like the popular Pennington Wild Bird Food from The Home Depot.

Plain, unsalted peanuts might be the best thing in the pantry for birds preparing for winter. Raw or dry-roasted, unsalted nuts are packed with heart-healthy fats and dense proteins that small birds need to bulk up reserves ahead of winter. Peanuts, walnuts, pecans, and almonds also attract an enthusiastic crowd, including tufted titmice, black-capped chickadees, woodpeckers, and blue jays. Jays in particular will happily carry off whole shelled peanuts to stash in tree hollows and mulch beds.

Never offer nuts that contain added salt, spicy seasonings, sugar glazes, or chocolate. Birds have minimal tolerance for sodium and cannot process salty cocktail party leftovers. Crush or chop whole nuts into coarse pieces, so smaller songbirds like chickadees and nuthatches can eat them safely. And keep a lookout for any that smell musty or stale and remove quickly to prevent infection. The very affordable Round Peanut Bird Feeder from Amazon is a novel way of dishing up your nuts.

Rice has a reputation for swelling up and bursting birdie tummies. But this myth has been debunked by ornithologists. Plenty of wild birds (like doves and bobwhites) eat rice. However, from a nutritional standpoint, plain cooked rice is the superior choice for backyard songbirds. Steamed brown or white rice leftovers offer quick carbs that are easy for house sparrows, doves, rock pigeons, and common grackles to digest.

The rice must be cooked with zero butter, cooking oils, salt, soy sauce, garlic, or onions. Also, damp rice is susceptible to bacterial contamination, so only put out a few tablespoons at a time on cool mornings. Sweep away uneaten grains each day to keep your feeding station rodent-free. Rice is a tasty snack, but supplement with high protein treats. You can buy Kaytee Dried Mealworms from Walmart.

Slightly squishy blueberries, raspberries, blackberries, or strawberries that might be lingering in the fridge crisper drawer are a scrummy treat for birds. In nature, wild berries are rich in antioxidants, vitamin C, and simple sugars that provide instant fuel. Northern mockingbirds, eastern bluebirds, and American robins will find fresh berries irresistible as natural hedgerow fruit diminishes. And a flock of cedar waxwings may empty a tray by lunch.

Serve berries fresh and unseasoned, slicing larger strawberries into quarters. Only place small portions on a clean feeding platform early in the day, as high-moisture berries degrade rapidly. If you’re after a standing bird feeder that can hold fruits and keep them better protected from rain, the charming Ontala Metal Bird Feeder and Bath with Umbrella, available from Amazon, is great value and a real talking point. A word of warning if you are a dog owner: never substitute fresh berries with dried raisins or currants. They cause kidney failure in canines, even in tiny quantities.

When preparing dinner, set aside a small portion of plain baked, boiled, or steamed potatoes before adding butter, milk, or seasoning. Boiled potato is fine in small amounts if nothing's been added to it. It provides easy starch on freezing mornings. Starlings, common grackles, jays, and robins will happily pick apart soft potato cubes when natural insect foraging grounds become frozen and inaccessible.

Prep your bird-friendly spuds by chopping them into tiny, crumbly, pea-sized bits so they are easy for birds to ingest. However, never feed birds raw potatoes or any green-skinned bits. These contain solanine, which causes gastrointestinal distress and neurological damage in birds. And avoid french fries, salty potato chips, or buttery mashed potatoes. To supplement your potato with a “meaty” treat, hang out some suet. Placed in cages, like the More Birds Double Suet Feeder with Weather Guard from Amazon, this gives a nourishing fall boost to prime birds for winter chills.

This is prime pumpkin-carving season, leaving behind mounds of gooey seeds that are often destined for the trash. But fresh pumpkin seeds, butternut squash seeds, and raw sunflower seeds are nutrient powerhouses for backyard wildlife. They are loaded with raw fats, plant proteins, and magnesium, all of which cardinals, chickadees, titmice, nuthatches and blue jays need now.

Place the seeds in a colander, rinse away any stringy pulp and spread in a single layer on a parchment-lined baking sheet to air-dry for 24-48 hours. Leave them raw and unsalted. To help smaller beaks, run your dry seeds through a food processor for a few pulses to crack the husks. If you need to, you can grab a bag of National Audubon Society Black Oil Sunflower Seed from Lowe’s to bulk up these free treats as they are sure to go fast.

Some leftovers belong in the trash, however cold it gets. The theobromine in chocolate is toxic to birds. Avocado is another hard no, as it can cause heart damage and death. Salty snacks and cured meats need to stay inside, plus anything cooked with onion or garlic. Bread is a bit of a gray area, as it isn't harmful, but it fills a bird up without much fat or protein.

Bacon grease trips people up. It seems like a handy base for treats, but it's salty and carries preservatives. It also stays soft, and soft fat smeared on feathers can damage their waterproofing. For a safe birdie snack along similar lines, opt for suet cakes that are designed for the job. The double-basket Woodlink Suet Basket from Walmart holds two cakes, handy for when woodpeckers and nuthatches line up in the cold.

Making more of kitchen scraps feels great in terms of recycling, and it can also help you save a little on multiple bird food products. It also means you have a bit more cash freed up to treat yourself and your local birdlife to a pretty feeder. Plenty of options offer smart functionality and real-time footage of your feeding friends. These curated picks are some of the best for aesthetics, value for money and bird-friendly features, letting you feast your eyes on your feathered pals while they chow down.

Currently a whopping third off the normal price, this bargain smart feeder can identify over 6000 species of birds and can even distinguish males from females. Users love the easy assembly and sturdy build, as well as the garden-friendly mocha accents.

Combine function and visual elegance with this pretty 2-in-1 feeder and solar light. Perfect for cardinals, it has a classy vintage Mediterranean vibe, good drainage, and a lovely splashguard.

Crisp action shots, instant notifications, and 2K video are just a few attractions with this feeder camera, and it even tells you when to expect birdie visits for specific species. Great camera quality, super easy to use, and currently available at a 20% discount.

Supplementing your fall bird feeding with these kitchen scraps is a great way to reduce household waste while giving local wildlife a crucial calorie boost. Just remember they are designed to serve as supplements rather than replacements to your existing bird feeds. Make sure you offer a diverse natural diet this fall, and combine these scraps with fresh water, to keep your backyard birdies thriving and happy all season long.

My 1-year-old cat Daisy has allergies. She is on a special hydrolyzed diet. Iâm trying to find an allergen-neutralizing spray to cut back on dust mites in the house. Would you recommend any specific products?

Since Daisy is already on a hydrolyzed diet, it makes sense to look at environmental allergens too, especially if her allergic signs are continuing. Dust mites are common household allergens, and while the goal is to reduce the amount of allergens in her environment, eliminating them completely is not realistic. Regularly washing bedding and blankets, vacuuming with a HEPA filter, and keeping dust to a minimum are still the best places to start.

If you would like to try a spray, Purefy Anti-Allergen Spray works differently from an insecticide. It is intended to neutralize or remove the allergenic proteins associated with dust mite debris, particularly the proteins found in their feces and other microscopic particles that accumulate in household dust and fabrics. Those proteins, rather than the living mite itself, are an important source of the allergic reaction. So the idea is not to kill every mite in the house, but to reduce the allergen they leave behind.

I would specifically avoid routinely using insecticide or acaricide sprays around Daisy, even when a product is marketed as ânatural.â Cats can be particularly sensitive to certain botanical ingredients and insecticides, including some essential oils and pyrethroids. If you use an anti-allergen spray, follow the label carefully, keep Daisy away from treated surfaces until they are completely dry, ventilate the area well, and never spray it directly on her or on surfaces she is likely to lick. Please ensure you also keep it away from food and water bowls.

Think of the spray as an extra layer of environmental control, not a treatment for Daisy's allergy. The unglamorous combination of washing, HEPA vacuuming, and reducing dust is still doing most of the heavy lifting. And if Daisy continues to have significant allergic signs despite a properly conducted hydrolyzed diet trial and environmental management, it is worth investigating other possible triggers rather than simply reaching for stronger household chemicals. Usually, the answer is not a more powerful spray, but figuring out exactly what is making your cat itchy. So, real detective work is often needed for success.

#7852. Ask Dr. Paola - HELP! What Happens If Cherry Eye Is Left Untreated? (November 2, 2026)

Welcome to our "Ask Dr. Paola" series, where every other Monday we bring expert advice straight from Dr. Paola Cuevas (MVZ) to help our readers better understand their dog's health and well-being.

Whether you're a new pet parent or a seasoned dog lover, Dr. Paola is here to provide answers to your most pressing questions. From nutrition tips and preventive care to troubleshooting common behavioral issues, Dr. Paola is ready to offer insights that will keep your furry friend happy and healthy. Stay tuned for expert guidance on a range of topics that matter most to you and your dog, so you can make informed decisions and provide the best possible care for your canine companion.

âHaveâ a âquestion? Send it in here!

My dog, Reggie, has Cherry eye. If left untreated, can it have a negative effect on his vision? Money is an issue for me right now.â

Cherry eye happens when the gland of the third eyelid, which helps produce tears, slips out of its normal position and becomes visible as a pink or red cherry-looking bulge in the corner of your dog's eye. I understand that veterinary expenses can be difficult to manage, and it is important to know what needs attention right away and what can safely wait a bit longer.

Cherry eye does not usually cause blindness directly, but leaving it untreated can put Reggie's eye health at risk. The exposed gland can become irritated, inflamed, or damaged, and its tear production may be reduced over time. Because this gland contributes to keeping the eye moist and protected, reduced tear production can increase the risk of dry eye, a condition that can lead to corneal damage, scarring, and impaired vision if it becomes severe. Think of the gland as part of the eye's built-in lubrication system. Even if the eye looks comfortable today, problems can develop gradually.

If surgery is not financially possible right now, please arrange a veterinary examination to confirm the diagnosis, assess tear production, and check the cornea.

Talk to your vet about a payment plan, or you might be able to find a veterinary teaching hospital or nonprofit clinic that may offer lower-cost care. Your veterinarian may recommend a suitable lubricating eye product while you work toward surgery, but lubrication will not reposition the gland. Please make sure you avoid human eye drops, leftover medications, or steroid eye drops unless specifically prescribed, as some of these can worsen an undiagnosed corneal ulcer. The gland should generally be repositioned and preserved rather than removed. If the gland is removed, you would need to use eye drops to supplement Reggieâs tear production for the rest of his life.

Please seek same-day veterinary care if you see Reggie squinting, holding the eye closed, rubbing it persistently, developing a cloudy or bluish cornea, or producing thick yellow or green discharge. These can be signs of a painful or more serious eye problem. If the eye is comfortable and clear, it may not be an immediate emergency, but I would not leave cherry eye unassessed for weeks or months. The most important first step is protecting the eye while finding an affordable treatment option.

A spider plant with browning leaves at this time of the year is a desperate cry for help – here’s what to do to save your airplane plant, pronto!

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If your spider plant has brown leaf tips this fall, you should take action, fast. Brown leaf tips on a spider plant are like the warning lights on your car dashboard: they alert you to a problem that, if you don’t do something about it, is likely to get far worse. In fall, dying leaf tips are a common houseplant complaint, but it’s vital to work out what the problem behind this symptom is so you can set it right and bring your Chlorophytum comosum back to full health.

Don’t worry, though. A spider plant with brown leaf tips is easily fixed if you act soon enough, so great work getting here to Garden ER where you'll find straightforward solutions to treat this season’s biggest planty problems. The localized damage you see as brown leaf tips on a spider plant isn’t life-threatening in its own right, but it could be pointing to a problem that is potentially fatal. So, taking swift action if you spot browning leaf tips is an important part of fall houseplant care.

Come on in and let’s diagnose and treat your poorly spider plant with browning leaves.

First off, take a closer look at your spider plant’s dead leaf tips. Is there a clean, sharp line between the brown and the green leaf parts, or can you see a thin yellow section between them? Is the browning just at the tip of the leaves or are there any dark patches near the center or base of those leaves? Do the brown areas feel dry or mushy to the touch, and is the discoloration a dull greyish, blackish brown or a warmer, redder brown? The answers to these questions will help to inform your diagnosis.

In fall, there are four likely culprits behind a spider plant's browning leaves, and your foliage examination will help you work out which it is. Remember, your houseplant may be stressed by more than one issue so may show more than one type of damage.

Turning on a home’s heating system in fall is a common reason why spider leaf tips turn brown in fall. This is the likely cause if the damaged foliage feels dry and crispy, and there’s a sharp line between the green parts and the discolored leaf tips, or a very narrow, clean yellow line separating them. When the heat gets turned on, the air in your home rapidly loses its humidity and in these drier conditions, moisture can evaporate from a spider plant’s leaves faster than roots can replace it. As a spider plant primarily loses most moisture from its leaf tips, that's where the damage shows first.

When days start to shorten, spider plants dramatically slow their growth rate, so need to drink far less water. If you haven’t adjusted your watering routine to suit, the plant is likely getting more water than it can use. Roots are likely stressed as they’re sitting in wet, soggy soil, and this damage shows up as yellowing leaves and a blurry-edged yellow halo-like zone separating the green and brown leaf parts. This damage can appear anywhere on the leaf and, if the patches feel mushy and extend into the center or base of the leaf then those houseplant roots have started to rot.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Spider plants hail from tropical climates so if yours is sitting on a windowsill or near an external door where it's regularly blasted by cold air, it will likely struggle as temperatures drop outdoors. If this is the problem, then leaves will become floppy, dull and pale, and any foliage that’s touching a glass window pane will rapidly turn brown or black, often overnight, and feel soft and limp.

Spider plants are tough houseplants but they don’t cope well with tap water that’s high in fluoride and chlorine. And while this is a year-round problem, when a spider plant is dealing with fall-induced environmental stress on top of this chemical stress, the issue can quickly become obvious.

Spider plants pull water – and any fluoride and chlorine in it – to their leaf tips, where much of the water evaporates, leaving a concentration of chemicals. This causes browning that starts at the very tip of the leaf and creeps down the outside edges. A distinctive reddish-brown tint is another diagnostic clue to tap-water chemicals being the cause. The discoloration on the outer, older leaves will be worse than on the inner, younger leaves which haven't been sucking up the chemicals for as long. Brown leaf tips will feel dry and crispy, you may see a narrow yellow line between the green and brown parts, and there might be a crusty white residue on the soil or inner rim of the pot.

All these problems are easily fixed with the right spider plant care.

Check your spider plant isn’t sitting too close to a radiator, heat vent or in a current of warm air. Moving it to a more humid room such as a bathroom will help it recover, or stand the pot on a shallow tray of water and pebbles such as this Bonsai Humidity Tray from Lowe’s, or make your own with an old plant saucer and pea gravel like this Landscape Rock from Walmart. Make sure the pot base sits on top of the pebbles rather than in the water – you’re simply using the water to humidify the air as it evaporates.

Stop watering immediately, let the soil dry out and only water when the top inch of potting mix feels dry, or take out the guesswork with a moisture meter like this from Amazon.

If you suspect root rot, slide the pot off and if there’s a foul, stagnant smell, however faint, you’ll need to take action to save your plant. Remove as much soil as possible and use sharp pruners or scissors to snip off any rotting roots that are dark in color, mushy or slimy. Rinse the roots and wash the pot, then repot your spider plant with a fast-draining potting mix like Back to the Roots Organic Succulents & Cacti Mix, available from The Home Depot.

Move your plant to a spot with bright but indirect sunlight – a room with an east- or west-facing window is ideal.

Switch to using harvested rainwater or distilled water. Don’t use regular filtered water because while a filter removes chlorine, fluoride slips right through. A gallon jug of distilled water costs just over a dollar from Walmart and will keep your spider plant watered for 3 months, and rainwater is even cheaper! It’s also a wise idea to repot your spider plant into fresh potting soil to remove any build-up of chemicals sitting around the roots, or flush or leach the existing soil by pouring rain- or distilled water through.

Trim damaged leaf tips with sharp scissors, cutting at an angle to mimic the pointed shape of the foliage.

Sheikhdoon Abdullahi Mohamud, 18, of Richfield, Minnesota, was charged today by complaint with one count of knowingly receiving a firearm and ammunition in order to commit a federal crime of terrorism.

The FBI arrested the defendant on Oct. 6, and he made his initial appearance before U.S. Magistrate Judge Elizabeth Cowan Wright on Oct. 7.

“This individual allegedly obtained a weapon he hoped to use in a mass casualty attack in support of ISIS, but this FBI arrested him and put a stop to his plans,” said FBI Director Kash Patel. “Once again this FBI is moving more effectively than we ever have before at stopping terrorists before they can attack Americans – with over 1,100 individuals prevented from conducting attacks, over 4,000 foreign terrorist organization related disruptions and arrests, a 38% increase, and more. We will continue to use every resource we have to detect and prevent acts of terrorism and wipe out their networks all over the country. Thank you to FBI Minneapolis who did an outstanding job in the investigation and likely saved lives.”

“Mohamud allegedly sought to carry out a mass-casualty shooting at the Mall of America, expressing a desire to emulate some of the most horrific ISIS-inspired attacks in the United States, including the atrocities at Pulse Nightclub and 2025 New Year’s Day attack in New Orleans,” said Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg. “The National Security Division will continue to work closely with the FBI and Joint Terrorism Task Force to track down and prosecute ISIS-inspired terrorists in the United States.”

“As alleged in the criminal complaint, Mohamud took substantial steps to plot to murder innocent people in the name of ISIS,” said U.S. Attorney Daniel N. Rosen for the District of Minnesota. “Such threats are taken seriously, and I commend the committed public servants of the Joint Terrorism Task Force, the FBI, and my office, who work every day to stop them.”

According to the complaint, beginning in or about December 2024, Mohamud exchanged hundreds of messages through multiple social media and messaging applications with a confidential source. Mohamud expressed his desire to travel to Somalia to join a designated foreign terrorist organization to fight on its behalf. Mohamud also expressed a desire to commit a mass-casualty event in Minnesota by acquiring and using a firearm and ammunition. The defendant stated many times that if he was unable to travel overseas because of a lack of funds, he planned to carry out a mass-casualty event in Minnesota in support of ISIS.

In July 2026, Mohamud sent messages discussing his intent to carry out a mass-casualty shooting attack at the Mall of America because he claimed it was owned by Jews. He wrote that wanted to kill 30 to 60 people so no one would go there.

In August and September 2026, Mohamud continued to send messages discussing his intentions, including his plans to purchase a firearm and to recruit others to join him in committing the attack. Mohamud sent a selfie-style video of himself pledging allegiance to ISIS:

During the course of his communications, Mohamud stated that he wanted to commit an attack similar to those of the Pulse Nightclub mass-shooting in Orlando, the Bondi Beach mass-shooting in Australia, and the New Year’s Day vehicle-ramming attack in New Orleans.

In September 2026, Mohamud expressed a desire to kill “kuffar” — a term used to refer to a non-Muslim. Mohamud identified Oct. 24 as the date of his planned attack. When the confidential source asked if there was a big gathering on Oct. 24, Mohamud indicated that there were would be numerous Asians and other “kuffar” celebrating at the Mall of America. Mohamud then sent a link to a “Hmong Arts Celebration” at the Mall of America.

In September 2026, Mohamud continued to send propaganda videos to the confidential source. A still shot from one of the propaganda videos sent by Mohamud is depicted below:

On Oct. 6, the FBI arranged to sell to Mohamud, through an undercover FBI employee, an AK-47 assault rifle, four 30-round magazines, and approximately 200 rounds of ammunition. The FBI rendered the AK-47 rifle inert prior to the transaction. The FBI arrested Mohamud shortly after he paid about $600 cash for the rifle, magazines, and ammunition and had those items in his possession. During the sale of the firearm and ammunition, Mohamud reaffirmed his plan to use the firearm and ammunition to shoot people at the Mall of America.

This case was the result of an investigation by the FBI, the Joint Terrorism Task Force, and the Bloomington Police Department, with assistance from IRS Criminal Investigation.

This case is being prosecuted by Trial Attorney Ryan White of the National Security Division’s Counterterrorism Section and Assistant U.S. Attorney Benjamin Bejar for the District of Minnesota.

A complaint is merely an allegation. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.
