#7781. How Wolford v. Lopez Refines Second Amendment Doctrine

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Court's rejection of the Vampire Rule has broad implications

The Supreme Court's June decision in Wolford v. Lopez prevented the obliteration of the right to bear arms in five States, holding that governments may not make carrying a licensed handgun presumptively illegal almost everywhere. 609 U.S. 185 (2026).  Important as the result is, perhaps of even greater significance is how Wolford clarified Second Amendment doctrine. According to Wolford:

Determining whether a challenged law falls within the "plain text" of the Amendment is much simpler than some lower courts and gun control advocates have claimed.

Modern gun control laws do not always have to be justified by analogies from past practices, but analogies cannot be based on oddities and outliers.

Racist gun control laws from the past, which were long ago repudiated by constitutional amendment, are not valid precedents for infringing the rights of modern Americans.

This essay will also discuss the Hawaii Attorney General's argument that only a weak version of the Second Amendment should apply in the Aloha State. And the argument that Hawaii's "Vampire Rule" to prohibit licensed carry throughout the State did not even implicate the Second Amendment.

In a constitutional case, the court must decide if the challenged government action involves a constitutional provision. Often the issue is simple; for example, a public meeting about a political controversy is an example of "the right  . . . to assemble."

In edge cases, judges may have to decide how literally to read the text. For example, the First Amendment protects "the freedom of speech," and while Justice Hugo Black was often absolutist in his protection of literal "speech" (saying words out loud), he disagreed with Supreme Court majorities that gave "freedom of speech" protection to conduct. E.g., Cox v. Louisiana, 379 U.S. 559, 578 (1965) (Black, J., concurring in part and dissenting in part) ("Picketing, though it may be utilized to communicate ideas, is not speech, and therefore is not of itself protected by the First Amendment.").

For the Second Amendment, the textual inquiry is, "When the Second Amendment's plain text covers an individual's conduct, the Constitution presumptively protects that conduct." New York State Rifle & Pistol Assoc. v. Bruen, 597 U.S. 1, 24 (2022).

Unfortunately, some lower courts did not take the "plain text" language seriously, and began importing all sorts of rules into the plain text determination. For example, the "plain text" of "the right of the people" was said to require proof that the individuals were "law-abiding" and "responsible." The plain text of "Arms" was said to require proof that the arms in question were frequently "used" (such as gun being fired, or a knife being used to cut) for self-defense. I described some of the misapplications of "plain text" in a 2024 post, How Some Courts are Evading Bruen by Changing its Rules: Lower Courts evading the "plain text" of the Second Amendment.

The Wolford Court showed that the plain text inquiry is not nearly so complicated as some of the lower courts had claimed. In fact, there are just three simple questions:

Question 1: Because the Second Amendment guarantees "the right of the people," the court must ask if the law applies to "the people"— that is, to members of the American political community. The Court here contradicts the notion of some lower courts that "the people" excludes various subsets of the American people — such as persons under 21 years old, or persons who have been convicted of a crime. While some of the American people can be restricted in their Second Amendment rights, all Americans start with the right, and it is up to government to justify the deprivation. The justification, however, comes later in a case, and is not part of the plain text inquiry.

Question 2: The class of "Arms" covered by the plain text is very broad: "any weapon customarily used for offensive or defensive purposes." Again, this is the plain-text step only. Just as some members of "the people" may lawfully be disarmed, some weapons (e.g., machine guns) may be found not to be protected by the Second Amendment right. Any determination that particular persons or arms fall outside the Amendment's protection comes later in the case, not in the plain-text inquiry.

The Wolford Court's rule implicitly rebukes some lower courts that had ruled that "Arms" in the Second Amendment's plain excludes all arms related to military arms. Or that "Arms" includes only weapons that the challengers prove to be frequently used for self-defense against criminal attacks in progress.

The term "customarily" does not mean "most often." For example, the number of times that handgun triggers are pressed for target shooting competitions vastly exceeds the number of times that handguns are fired at criminal attackers.

Question 3: As for "any restrictions" on "possession" or "carrying" of arms, some lower courts may continue their current very narrow readings, holding that laws such as bans on gun stores do not implicate the Second Amendment's plain text at all — even though acquiring arms is a prerequisite to  possession and carry.

The Wolford majority found that Hawaii's Vampire Rule easily passed all three questions. The law affected American citizens with Hawaii carry permits, and those Hawaiians are among "the people." The law applied to carrying handguns, which are customarily used for defense. And the law made it pervasively illegal to carry licensed handguns in public.

"If a challenged law falls within the plain text of the Second Amendment, it is presumptively unconstitutional—which means that it may violate the preexisting right that the Amendment codified. But because that right was not in every way coterminous with the Amendment's literal language, further analysis may be needed. Specifically, the relevant government—federal, state, or local—may be able to show that its challenged law did not infringe the historical understanding of the codified right."

"A variety of sources, including scholarship, may aid this inquiry. But often, the best evidence may be what Bruen called historical analogues. These are old legal rules from which a court may draw a strong inference that the modern law at issue is consistent with the codified right. A party defending against a Second Amendment claim may rely on a single analogue or a group of analogues." (citations omitted).

Building on and clarifying Bruen's discussion of historical analogues, the Wolford Court explained that Bruen had "identified three important inquiries that courts should undertake in evaluating proffered analogues."

"The first is the number of jurisdictions in which they were adopted. . . . When we assess whether a challenged law is consistent with the right the Second Amendment codified, we seek the general understanding of that codified right at the relevant point in time. An outlier legal rule adopted in a few locales is not enough."

"The second is the extent to which they were well-accepted. This acceptance may be express, as when judicial decisions explicitly acknowledged the rule's legality. Or the acceptance may be tacit, as when a restriction on the keeping or carrying of arms was 'open, widespread, and unchallenged.'" (Quoting Bruen).

Inquiries one and two add some specificity to the Bruen rule of "a well-established and representative historical" analogue.

"The third is whether any analogue or collection of analogues is 'relevantly similar' to the modern law."

Determining whether an analogue is "relevantly similar" requires consideration of "how" it restricted the keeping or bearing of arms. "And a court must also consider 'why' the analogue restricted the keeping or bearing of arms—that is, whether its rationale was similar to that of the new law."

As seen in other cases, the "how" and "why" inquiries often involve "who." For example, some 18th- and 19th-century surety laws required an individual to post bond for peaceable behavior if the individual had been found by a court to be potentially dangerous. In United States v. Rahimi, the Court's majority found surety laws to be relevant analogues for modern laws disarming persons who have been issued a domestic violence restraining order based on an individualized judicial finding of danger to a past or present domestic partner. 602 U.S. 680 (2024). In Bruen, however, the surety laws were not relevant analogues for state laws preventing almost everyone from carrying firearms.

A standard argument in favor of originalism is that while it does not conclusively resolve every issue, it constrains judicial decisions more than do alternative methods. In Wolford's words, "Making this determination is far more disciplined than the 'interest-balancing,' 'judge-empowering' standard that Heller emphatically rejected, but it is not mechanical." The Court added, "It undeniably necessitates an exercise of judgment."

In Wolford's words, "Making this determination is far more disciplined than the 'interest-balancing,' 'judge-empowering' standard that Heller emphatically rejected, but it is not mechanical." "It undeniably necessitates an exercise of judgment," the Court added,

For example, in the three cases where the Court has applied Bruen and examined analogies, the Court was unanimous in one, and divided in two others: United States v. Hemani, 146 S.Ct. 1677 (2026) (9-0) (historical vagrancy, civil-commitment, and surety laws concerning habitual drunkards who had lost the capacity for self-control were inadequate analogues for prosecuting a gun owner based on his regular marijuana use); United States v. Rahimi (8-1) (historic laws, such as sureties, against persons proven to be dangerous are sufficient analogues for modern laws that go even further, such as by felonizing firearms possession in the home); Wolford v. Lopez (6-3) (as described below, laws against poachers or Black people are not analogues for preventing everyone from carrying firearms).

Applying Wolford's rules for analogues to the Vampire Rule

The Supreme Court's Bruen decision had directly applied to three States where licensed carry was almost completely prohibited (Hawaii, Maryland, New Jersey) and to three where it was prohibited by some local jurisdictions and allowed in others (California, New York, Massachusetts). After Bruen, all of the above states, except Massachusetts, enacted a law that had been proposed by University of Alabama law professor Fredrick Vars and Yale law professor Ian Ayres; as they frankly stated, the purpose of the law was to make licensed carry extremely inconvenient, and thereby discourage people with carry licenses from using those licenses.

Under the Hawaiian statute, a person with a concealed handgun carry permit "shall not . . . enter or remain on private property of another person . . ." while carrying a loaded or unloaded firearm "unless the person has been given express authorization" by the owner, lessee, operator, manager, or other person authorized under the statute. The "express authorization" must be "Unambiguous written or verbal authorization" or "clear and conspicuous signage at the entrance." Private property meant all property other than the permit holder's own property, or government property. Hawaii Revised Statutes § 134-9.5.

Separately, and not at issue in Wolford, the Hawaiian legislature's Bruen response law had outlawed licensed carry on most government property and vast swaths of private property by labeling them "sensitive places."

The Wolford plaintiffs challenged the Hawaii "express authorization" statute as it applied to business premises that are open to the public. As of the time that the Court was considering Wolford, similar laws were held unconstitutional by the Second, Third, and Fourth Circuits. Antonyuk v. James, 120 F.4th 941 (2d Cir. 2024); Koons v. Attorney General of New Jersey, 156 F.4th 210 (3d Cir. 2025); Kipke v. Moore, 165 F.4th 194 (4th Cir. 2026). But the Ninth Circuit had come to an opposite result. Wolford v. Lopez, 116 F.4th 959 (2024). The Supreme Court granted certiorari, perhaps influenced by a U.S. Solicitor General amicus brief in support of the petition.

Critics of the express authorization rule call it the "Vampire Rule," because in some stories, vampires can only enter certain buildings when invited. The history of the Vampire Rule in literature was detailed in my amicus brief, which I coauthored on behalf of the National Rifle Association and the Independence Institute. While vampires are malignant and dangerous, Hawaii's Vampire Rule "applies only to beings who are exceptionally not dangerous: law-abiding citizens who have passed a background check, completed safety training, and have been licensed by the government to carry concealed handguns." The brief provided empirical evidence of the extremely low rate of gun misuse by persons with carry permits, compared to the general population. The brief also described the legality, in the Founding Era, of carrying on private property that was open to the public. That part of the brief was cited by the United States and by petitioners' counsel during oral argument (pages 50, 125).

Most of the analogues proffered by the Hawaii Attorney General in support of the Vampire Rule were colonial and Founding Era anti-poaching laws that forbade armed trespassers from entering other persons' enclosed farms or pastures without consent. Justice Alito's majority opinion found the purported analogy preposterous:

"To test whether these analogues are 'relevantly similar' to the challenged Hawaii law, we may ask the question set out earlier: 'Because it was accepted that prohibiting unauthorized hunting on private land was consistent with the Second Amendment right, can we infer that it is also consistent with that right to ban a person who is lawfully carrying a concealed handgun for self-defense from entering a gas station, coffee shop, grocery store, or other private property open to the public without express and unambiguous consent?' The question answers itself. The gap between the State's anti-poaching analogues and its new rule is just too wide."

Justice Barrett joined the majority opinion, and also wrote a concurrence. In her analysis:

"So the problem with Hawaii's default rule is not that it targets a regulatory problem besides poaching. It is that the rule does not target any particular abuse of firearms at all. Rather than identifying a specific threat to public peace and safety, Hawaii admits that it enacted the rule because many of its citizens oppose the public carry of guns. In other words, Hawaii is responding to the general danger associated with the presence of firearms, not to any specific, heightened risk of their misuse."

"Mere disapproval of protected conduct is not a valid reason to severely restrict it."

The Hawaii Attorney General pointed to an 1893 Oregon statute against carrying arms on enclosed premises or lands without the consent of the owner. While the Hawaii Attorney General claimed that the statute applied to business premises, there was no indication that such an interpretation had ever been used in Oregon.

"But even if this provision is read as Hawaii would have it, a lone statute adopted nearly a century after the adoption of the Second Amendment and well after the adoption of the Fourteenth Amendment sheds little if any light on the meaning of the Second Amendment right," wrote the Wolford Court.

The Wolford Court's disparaging treatment of far-fetched (poaching) or isolated and very late (Oregon 1893) analogues did not break new ground. What does significantly affect Second Amendment doctrine is the Court's treatment of the 1865 Louisiana Black Code. Ever since Bruen was decided, anti-gun advocates and some lower court judges have been pointing to laws against enslaved people or against free people of color as supposed justifications for modern laws aimed at other groups of people, or at the public in general.

After the Civil War ended with Confederate surrender in April 1865, everyone could see that abolition was coming, and the former slave States would soon have large populations of newly free Black people. The 1865 Louisiana legislature enacted a statute that really did match the scope of Hawaii's Vampire Rule. As the Wolford Court explained:

"Finally, we come to the State's most remarkable analogue, an 1865 Louisiana statute that made it unlawful 'for any person or persons to carry fire-arms on the premises or plantations of any citizen, without the consent of the owner or proprietor, other than in lawful discharge of a civil or military order.' 1865 La. Acts No. 10, § 1, p. 14. Regardless of this provision's pedigree, it has no probative value for present purposes. As we have said, in considering the probative value of a historical analogue, we must consider whether it was widespread, well-known, and widely accepted. See Bruen, 597 U.S. at 35. Because this statute was neither widespread nor widely accepted, it carries no weight."

"We could stop there, but there is another reason for rejecting Hawaii's reliance on this statute. It was adopted by the Louisiana Legislature between the end of the Civil War and the beginning of Reconstruction. When the war ended, the legislatures in defeated Confederate States quickly enacted so-called Black Codes that aimed to perpetuate the subjugation of blacks. The statute Hawaii cites was part of Louisiana's Black Code, and it provided a tool for disarming blacks and thus leaving them defenseless against attacks. See 125 F.4th at 1239 (VanDyke, J., dissenting from denial of reh'g en banc)."

"As we laid out in McDonald, the right to keep and bear arms was crucially important for vulnerable blacks during this period. See 561 U.S. at 757, 771, 776–779; id., at 843–846 (opinion of THOMAS, J.). And this was well-understood by the Republicans in Congress who were responsible for drafting, approving, and securing the ratification of the Fourteenth Amendment. The Republican Party Platforms of 1856 and 1860 called for protection of the right to keep and bear arms for self-defense. Unless we put history entirely out of our minds, Hawaii's claim that this tainted artifact illuminates the original understanding of the right to keep and bear arms cannot be taken seriously."

Concurring, Justice Barrett added, "The State seems to think Bruen is a matching game: Southern States enacted broad default rules, Hawaii reasons, so it can do the same today. But even if Hawaii is right that the how is analogous, it also must identify an analogous why. The Black Codes were enacted to subordinate newly freed slaves. Hawaii obviously does not contend that its law promotes an analogous interest." Therefore, the Hawaii law and the Black Codes were not relevantly similar.

Dissenting, Justice Jackson accurately described the doctrinal effect of the majority opinion: "it cuts Black Codes out of this country's tradition categorically and completely."

Yes, and properly so. As Bruen explained at length, the purpose of the judicial inquiry into "tradition" about the right to arms is not because tradition itself is the rule. Rather, tradition can shed light on original meaning. The original meaning of the Fourteenth Amendment includes how the constitutional right to arms was understood when passed by Congress in 1866 and ratified in 1868. As the Wolford majority pointed out with its citations to the extensive history provided by the majority and by Justice Thomas's concurrence in McDonald v. Chicago, the Fourteenth Amendment was meant to crush the Black Codes and the practices they perpetuated, including the obstruction of the right to arms.

Justice Jackson suggested that the Louisiana statute might have been facially compliant with the Second Amendment, the only problem being the discriminatory enforcement against Blacks. Tradition shows the opposite: not one law in American history before 1865 came close to such an outrageous nullification of the right to bear arms. (In a footnote, she cited the anti-poaching laws, which were not close to the Louisiana statute.)

Surprisingly, Justice Jackson's dissent claimed that the elimination of the Black Codes as precedents to justify modern gun control laws "deepens race-based wounds, by classifying the experiences of those who have been historically excluded as categorically irrelevant."

To the contrary, the Wolford majority follows the path laid down by McDonald:  classifying the experiences of persons who were historically excluded as of the highest categorical importance.  The Black Codes must never be forgotten or glossed over. The abuses (including extreme gun control) against them are an enduring negative example of what must never again be imposed in the United States.

Implications for other gun control laws based on prejudice

Wolford seems to do away with the precedential value of the post-Civil War Black Codes as affirmative historical support for modern gun restrictions. Its reasoning may also undermine reliance on antebellum race-based gun control laws targeting enslaved persons or free persons of color.

Justice Jackson asked "What do we do about other types of animus? For example, consider the use of statutes that were prejudiced against Catholics. See Kanter v. Barr, 919 F.3d 437, 457 (CA7 2019) (Barrett, J., dissenting). Does it offend history to use those?"

The Catholics question is easy to answer, based on text. The 1689 English Bill of Rights, which applied in British North America, protected only "Protestants." James Madison, however, wrote the Second Amendment without any religious restrictions. From American independence in 1776 onward, there appears to be no record of disarmament of Catholics — unlike the sizeable record of race-based disarmament.

Even before 1776, restrictions on Catholics in the future United States were rare. In 1756, during the French & Indian War, Virginia required Catholics to take a loyalty oath; if the oath were refused, arms would be confiscated for the militia, except for arms "necessary" for "the defence of his house or person." The same year, Pennsylvania confiscated "papist" arms and gave them to the colonial militia. In 1696, after an attempted assassination of King William III in England, the royal governor of New York confiscated the firearms of all ten Catholic men in the colony. For more, see Johnson, Kopel, Mocsary, Wallace, & Kilmer, Firearms Law and the Second Amendment 935 (Aspen Pubs. 4th ed. 2026); my Rahimi Amicus brief (for professors, including VC's Randy Barnett); my 2023 post, Old gun controls that were constitutionally repealed are not precedents for modern gun control; and my 2015 post, The Second Amendment versus anti-Catholicism.

"Aloha" should mean "goodbye" to Plessy v. Ferguson

Jim Crow jurisdictions justified themselves by reference to local conditions and tradition, which were supposedly accepted by almost everyone there. For example, Louisiana's 1890 Separate Car Act ordered railroads to place Blacks and Whites in separate cars. Upholding the Act, Justice Henry Billings Brown's majority opinion in  Plessy v. Ferguson described the Act as compliant with the "the established usages, customs, and traditions of the people." 163 U.S. 537 (1896).

But that wasn't true. The legislature had acted because the railroad companies refused to. The railroads preferred to segregate customers by sex, so that the men smoking cigars wouldn't foul the atmosphere for the women. Had customers preferred cars segregated by race rather than sex, the railroads presumably would have offered what was demanded. See, e.g., David Bernstein, Rehabilitating Lochner: Defending Individual Rights Against Progressive Reform (2011).

In Wolford, the Hawaii Attorney General made similar arguments to Justice Brown. Justice Jackson pointed an arms ban imposed in 1833 by King Kamehameha III. In a similar vein, the Hawaii Supreme Court declared that the Hawaii Constitution right to arms, which is worded identically to the U.S. Second Amendment, protects no right at all. The nullification was said to be justified by "the spirit of Aloha." State v. Wilson, 154 Haw. 8, 543 P.3d 440 (2024) ("Hawaiʻi's historical tradition of firearm regulation rule out an individual right to keep and bear arms under the Hawaiʻi Constitution.").

The Wolford majority replied that the Second Amendment, like everything else in the U.S. Constitution, applies equally in every State. "Merely local attitudes can neither shrink nor inflate the meaning of fundamental Bill of Rights guarantees that apply to the States through the Fourteenth Amendment." The Second Amendment is the same in "our 50th State (where about 8% of adults possess guns) and our 49th State [Alaska] (where the figure is roughly 59%)."

The principal dissent, by Justice Jackson and joined by Justice Sotomayor, argued that Wolford had nothing to do with the Second Amendment. It was just a property law case; because nobody has an inherent right to enter the property of another, Hawaii had merely changed a background rule about when consent could be presumed.

In fact, the inventors of the "default rule" (a/k/a Vampire Rule) created it for the express purpose of discouraging firearms carry by making it extremely difficult. See Ian Ayres & Fredrick E. Vars, Weapon of Choice: Fighting Gun Violence While Respecting Gun Rights (2020). They touted the rule in an op-ed published the month after the Bruen decision, pointing out the purpose of "substantially decreasing the places where concealed firearms can be carried." Ian Ayres & Fredrick Vars, "A new no-carry default for the U.S.: A gun law that could really change things," (New York) Daily News, July 20, 2022.

The Wolford majority chose not to blind itself to the law's purpose of massive suppression of the exercise of constitutional rights. To the majority, the dissent's argument that Hawaii had not infringed the Second Amendment:

"fails because States may not adopt property-law rules that violate constitutional rights. For example, a State may not adopt property-law rules that violate the freedom of speech. See, e.g., Reed v. Town of Gilbert, 576 U.S. 155, 159 (2015) (ordinance regulating signs on private property); City of Ladue v. Gilleo, 512 U.S. 43, 45 (1994) (similar). Nor may a State adopt zoning rules that violate the equal protection of the laws. See, e.g., Buchanan v. Warley, 245 U.S. 60 (1917). Likewise, a State may not "'sidestep the Takings Clause'" by enacting a law purporting to extinguish a property interest. Tyler v. Hennepin County, 598 U.S. 631, 638–639, (2023). The right protected by the Second Amendment is entitled to no less protection than other constitutional rights."

Justice Barrett's concurrence made similar points: "when a State enacts a property law that regulates arms-bearing conduct, that law implicates the Second Amendment."

"Consider how Hawaii and the principal dissent's argument would play out in another context. What if a State made it a crime to wear religious head garb (say, a hijab) onto private property open to the public without obtaining express authorization? Could that statute evade constitutional scrutiny? On Hawaii and the principal dissent's logic, the answer is apparently yes: No one has the right to enter another's property without permission, and the State has merely adjusted the default to require permission to be clear. But that is plainly wrong. Because the law regulates religious and expressive conduct, its enactment is state action that triggers First Amendment scrutiny. Cf. Martin v. City of Struthers, 319 U.S. 141, 143 (1943) (municipal ordinance prohibiting door-to-door solicitation violates the First Amendment)."

"The same goes for a default rule, like Hawaii's, that targets the right to bear arms. Property laws, no less than other laws, are subject to constitutional limits. So when a property law "restrict[s]" the bearing of arms, the State must prove that the law abides by the limits of the Second Amendment." (cross-references omitted).

"If Hawaii and the principal dissent were right that the Second Amendment does not kick in until a property owner gives consent, one wonders: Could a State simply prohibit its citizens from authorizing the carry of firearms onto their property? This would certainly interfere with the liberty of property owners, but it is hard to see how, on Hawaii and the principal dissent's logic, the Second Amendment would come into play."

David Kopel is research director at the Independence Institute.

#7778. The Real Reason Your Kitchen Smells (and What to Buy to Fix It)

Old Houses AREN’T Scary: What We’ve Learned & Loved About Them

Published Oct 27, 2026 2:26 PM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Your kitchen is supposed to be a place where you can gather to enjoy meals with family and friends. But if you walk into the room and are turned off by unpleasant smells, you may quickly lose your appetite. There are lots of reasons why your kitchen may be stinky. We spoke to a couple of cleaning experts to find out the most common sources of kitchen smells and how best to address them.

The sink itself is a common source of undesirable odors in the kitchen. “Many people regularly wipe down their countertops but neglect to clean the sink, which is constantly coated in food remains and liquids of all sorts,” says Ben Pullman, founder of Cubby Bear Cleaning in Chicago, Illinois. The best way to tackle this issue, says Pullman, is to simply clean the sink with some dish soap and a sponge after you’re done doing the dishes.

In addition, avoid throwing food scraps directly into the sink, recommends Arthuza Rabelo, a cleaning professional from Cleanzen Cleaning Services based in Boston, Massachusetts. “It’s better to use a sink strainer that catches small food particles and prevents them from going down the drain, as food scraps can accumulate in the pipes, cause blockages, and eventually produce unpleasant smells,” she says.

Finally, check the area under your sink as well, Rabelo adds. “Water damage in this area can cause a musty smell, similar to the odor of a damp cabinet floor,” she explains. If left unaddressed, it can also lead to mold or mildew growth and damage to the cabinet. “Make it a habit to inspect this area regularly so you can catch leaks early and prevent more serious damage, beyond just the unpleasant smell.” If you notice a leak, consult a professional as soon as possible.

Long-lasting, rust-proof stainless steel sink strainer with a double-layer design.

Although the trash can is one of the most obvious culprits of a smelly kitchen, there are steps to take to easily avoid this from happening. “The odor can come from the trash itself or the bin, which tends to get caked with residue over time,” says Pullman.

The best ways to combat this issue include taking your trash out more frequently, including as soon as it is full; replacing the garbage bag regularly; and cleaning the bin itself with a disinfecting wipe. Make sure to wipe down the inside of the bin as well as the lid, says Pullman. Also, avoid mixing biodegradable and non-biodegradable waste, as decomposing food can produce a strong odor that spreads throughout the kitchen, adds Rabelo.

Lysol Disinfecting Wipes are pre-moistened disposable wipes for cleaning, disinfecting, and sanitizing every surface in your home.

If there’s a new smell emanating from your kitchen, you’ll want to check all appliances to see if any of them are the cause. “Refrigerators, ovens, and other kitchen appliances are often sources of unpleasant smells,” notes Rabelo.

First, open the refrigerator to see if the stink is coming from inside. Expired, rotting food is often the cause of smells, says Pullman. “The best way to prevent it is to leave an open container of baking soda in the fridge at all times since it absorbs odors,” he adds. Aside from that, store food in sealed containers, regularly discard expired and old food, and wipe down the shelves and drawers of the fridge monthly, or even more frequently, with an all-purpose cleaner.

Next, check your microwave. “Especially if you’re heating up food without a cover, food tends to splatter in the microwave and even if it’s not a lot at once, over time it really builds up and starts to smell,” warns Pullman. “The best way to clean this is just using an all-purpose cleaner and a paper towel.”

Dishwashers can also pick up unwanted scents over time as a result of food particles getting trapped in the filter. After emptying the dishwasher, use a damp microfiber cloth to wipe off any debris on the floor and sides of the dishwasher’s interior. Next, fill a glass cup or bowl with about 1 cup of distilled white vinegar, and place it on the top rack of your dishwasher between the prongs used to separate glasses. Run the dishwasher through a single cycle on the hottest setting possible. Once the cycle is complete, leave the door open for about an hour to let the dishwasher air out completely.

Iberia Distilled White Vinegar has 5% acidity that can be used as a natural, eco-friendly cleanser for everyday tasks like wiping glass and counters.

The garbage disposal is another big one, as grinding food waste inevitably leaves the disposal smelling from time to time, says Pullman. Leftover food particles and soap residue often get stuck down in these areas or on the blades where bacteria can develop and produce a foul smell.

His favorite way to clean this is by cutting a lemon wedge, throwing it in the disposal, and grinding it up. “This works really well for most maintenance cleaning. If it requires more elbow grease, you can use some Bar Keeper’s Friend. Let it sit in there for 10 to 15 minutes, and then rinse and grind with hot water,” Pullman suggests. It’s a good idea to clean your garbage disposal on a weekly basis to prevent future stenches.

Concentrated powder cleanser that eliminates stubborn rust stains, cuts through grease, restores burnt pots and pans, and removes hard water deposits.

Grease and oil buildup from cooking can also start to smell. “When we cook, oil and sauces often splatter around the cooking area and gradually build up on nearby surfaces, especially the walls,” explains Rabelo. “Even if the smell isn’t too strong at first, this buildup can be one of the reasons your kitchen develops an unpleasant or unusual odor.”

He recommends making it a habit to wipe down the stove after each use, once it has cooled down. “Use a cloth with a little dishwashing liquid to clean the stove and surrounding areas, then wipe again with a damp cloth and finish with a dry one.” You can also prevent this from happening by using a splatter screen that has a carbon lining to absorb odors. Running your kitchen ventilation system will help manage the odor as well.

This gadget keeps stovetops and countertops clean when frying, while also controlling odor with its activated carbon filter.

Today the law firm of Weil Gotshal announced that it would wind down. I don't have any connections to the firm, though I did have one vignette to share that I wrote for another project. It concerns Greg Coleman, the first Texas Solicitor General.

In 2001, Coleman returned to Weil Gotshal to head his firm's Supreme Court practice. In 2006, Coleman took on a case that would change the face of constitutional law. He represented a municipal utility district from Northwest Austin, which challenged the constitutionality of Section 5 of the Voting Rights Act, known as the "preclearance requirement." This case had the potential to revolutionize voting rights, and bring our country closer to a colorblind Constitution. Unfortunately, Coleman's firm did not see things that way. As Senator Cruz recalled, "his partners at the firm lost their freaking minds." Coleman, who was dedicated to his client and the Constitution, left that firm and joined what would become Yetter Coleman LLP. In 2009, Coleman would argue two landmark Supreme Court cases that would set the stage for future constitutional restorations.

For many of us, November marks the beginning of a season filled with house guests, nonstop holiday cooking, and cozy nights indoors. It’s also the last chance for cold-region dwellers to finish last-minute outdoor maintenance and garden projects. Get ready for whatever this month brings by taking on these timely tasks.

Installing a programmable thermostat puts savings on automatic: It’s another task you won’t have to remember to do yourself. The U.S. Department of Energy estimates that homeowners can save about 10 percent on their heating costs by turning their thermostats down 7 to 10 degrees for eight hours a day. If you work outside the home, automatically setting your thermostat to a lower temperature while you’re gone should be a no-brainer. The Google Nest Learning Thermostat, the Best Overall pick in our tested guide to the best programmable thermostats, can be controlled via Alexa, Google Assistant, or the thermostat’s dial interface. If your home is on a septic system, this month is prime time to give it a little TLC. Dropping a septic tank treatment product into your toilet is an easy, effective DIY. We also like getting our septic tanks pumped in November, to ensure that there are no issues (remember that scene in Meet the Parents?) when we’re hosting company and our toilets are working overtime. In some areas, septic waste disposal fees increase on January 1, which gives you added incentive to take care of the task before the New Year.

Americans are getting ready to put their ovens and stovetops to work this month. Here’s an important reminder as you start your holiday prep: More cooking fires occur on Thanksgiving than on any other day of the year. Make sure you’re ready for whatever comes your way by keeping a fire extinguisher close at hand the kitchen, and letting the cooks know where it’s kept. Be sure to check the pressure of your current units, and replace old or damaged fire extinguishers.

The First Alert Kitchen5 weighs just under 1.5 pounds of dry chemical BC powder—typically enough to put out a small grease fire. Read the review.

There’s some debate over when to hang the Christmas lights, but many of us waste no time and flip the switch on Thanksgiving weekend. One of the best reasons to hang lights in November is that the (slightly) warmer weather makes this outside job easier to do. Whenever you choose to light up the yard, check all cords for fraying, and dispose of any damaged strings. Plug the lights into ground fault circuit interrupters (GFCIs) to reduce the risk of electrical fires, and turn them off before you go to sleep. We like the idea of hanging Govee’s outdoor strip lights, which you can leave up year-round and change the colors and patterns to suit different holidays. Our tested guide to the best Christmas lights has some other great choices, too.

When they are exposed to extreme temperatures, under- or non-insulated pipes, especially those that run along an exterior wall or an unheated garage, can freeze and cause major problems. To protect your pipes, first ensure that your walls are adequately insulated. You may also consider wrapping specialized heating cables or heating tape around water pipes that run along exterior walls. Heating tape can be plugged into an outlet, which will heat the water in your pipes to prevent freezing and bursting. Avoid installing heating tape inside walls, ceiling, or floors, where it can pose a fire hazard.

Gathering the family around the fireplace is one of the good things about cold weather. Before you strike a match, make sure you have plenty of firewood on hand for the season. Seasoned hardwood, like oak or ash, is generally the best wood for burning in the fireplace.

If you’ll be playing host to friends and family this season, now’s the time to get the guest bedroom in good shape. A fresh coat of paint or new bedding can make the space more inviting and won’t break the bank. Don’t have a spare bedroom? Alternative guest bed ideas, like cots, air mattresses, or pull-out sofas, can quickly turn any room into a bedroom.

Given the extra time you and your family will be spending in the kitchen through the end of the year, odds are higher that your countertops will see more spills, stains, and scratches than usual. The best ways to protect these surfaces depend on their composition: While materials like quartz and laminate only need regular cleaning with an all-purpose spray, countertops made of butcher block, marble, and granite should be sealed in order to resist stains (and warping, in the case of butcher block).

Once your countertops are protected, move on to cleaning your cutting boards: Plastic boards can be sanitized in the dishwasher; clean wood cutting boards with vinegar or, if stained, salt and half a lemon. Condition wood cutting boards with a food-safe mineral oil.

Your water heater is probably installed in an unheated environment, like a basement or a garage. Insulating your appliance is an absolute must to prevent it from losing heat. Choose an insulating water heater blanket that’s the right size for your tank, and follow the manufacturer’s instructions for installation. This quick task could save you 4 to 9 percent in water heating costs, and pay for itself in about a year.

Frost King’s water heater blanket is nonflammable, 3 inches thick, and provides an insulation value of R-10. Read the review.

Your kitchen will likely be getting a lot of use over the Thanksgiving holiday, which is why now is the time to minimize the risk of grease fires. Make sure to clean your stove drip pans and the stove top itself; go ahead and clean the oven, too, and whip up a nontoxic, fume-free mix of baking soda, water, and vinegar. Don’t use the self-clean function on your oven right before the big day: Self-cleaning puts strain on your appliance and could result in a maintenance call, or worse.

#7773. Your Home Flooded? Here’s Exactly What to Do Next To Minimize Damage

Parts of the U.S. are facing an increased risk of flooding. Here’s your no-panic playbook for if it ever happens to you.

As the warm air from a super el Niño makes its way across the North American continent, parts of the U.S. are facing increased risk of flooding in 2026 and 2027, according to Newsweek. The potential for disastrous wind and rain events during the winter is so great that the governor of California had already declared a statewide state of emergency as early as September. Southern states, from California to Florida, face the possibility of heavy rain, making flood response preparations even more important for people in these areas than in previous years.

Of course, you don’t have to wait for torrential rains to be at risk of flooding. A plumbing problem, like a toilet overflow, a burst pipe or a backed-up floor drain, can be just as serious. Whether your house flooded because of a natural disaster or a plumbing problem, timely response is of the essence to avoid mold and structural damage to your house and belongings as well as denials on your insurance claims.  The following checklist — informed by insurance and home restoration experts — will help you get ready.

“Water and electricity are the biggest immediate safety risk after a flood,” says damage remediation expert Sam Hickerson. Water flooding your basement or ground floor may come into contact with wall receptacles or other electrical equipment. If the power is still on, the water may be electrified.

Shut off the power yourself if you have a dry pathway to the main panel. If you have to wade through water to get to the panel, call the power company to have them do it remotely. Stay dry until you know the power is off.

Even after you’ve shut off the power, it’s important to stay out of the water, because it could be contaminated with sewage, animal waste and agricultural runoff. The bacteria, viruses and toxic chemicals these contaminants carry are obvious health hazards.

If the water is deep, there could be all sorts of debris in it that you can’t see, including broken glass and sharp metal. One false step, and you could suffer a cut that would be instantly infected if there are pathogens in the water.

“Many policies have specific windows for reporting flood damage, and delays can complicate a claim,” warns Hickerson. To avoid delays, call the insurance company as soon as it’s practical to do so and file a claim.

You don’t need to provide any details at this point; you’re just getting the claims process started. It will be the adjuster’s job to assess those details at some point in the (hopefully) near future.

Houston Chronicle/Hearst Newspapers/Getty Images

You’ll need photos to document the damage, and foundation repair specialist Shane McClintic recommends taking them before you start the cleanup. “Go around your house and film everything that suffered damage,” advises Gulf Coast flood insurance specialist Brad Spurgeon. “Once you have cleaned up your damage your pictures won’t be as useful to the insurance company.”

In particular, advises restoration expert Vinnie Guaderrama, take a picture of the highest point of water on the wall. “Always photograph the data plates with the model and serial numbers before you remove water heaters, furnaces, washers and dryers. Many people forget to do this, and it can be difficult to find these numbers at a later date.”

Try to have a restoration professional on site quickly. Restoration pros are in short supply during widespread disasters, however, so you might be working by yourself. If so, “work fast,” says McClintic.

According to the EPA, mold probably won’t grow on water-damaged materials if they dry within a 24-48 hour period. Once mold gets a foothold, it’s much harder to eradicate, so time is of the essence.

Because you need to work quickly to prevent mold from getting a foothold, water extraction should begin as soon as you can do it safely. “A wet/dry shop vac works for smaller amounts,” says Hickerson,  “but a sump pump is worth renting for anything beyond a few inches of standing water.”

When you can’t reach a hose into corners and under cabinets, don’t be afraid use a bucket and sponge to get the water out. Any standing water you leave will raise the room humidity and promote mold growth.

When you uncover previously submerged carpet, McClintic recommends either taking it outside or, if you can’t, pulling it back to air it out. “Prop up furniture on wood blocks to stop wicking,” advises Hickerson, “and pull baseboards, not just carpet, in flooded rooms.”

Drywall is a porous material that wicks water upward, and once waterlogged, you need to replace it. To avoid having to replace entire walls, McClintic advises cutting the drywall about a foot above the water line.

If you have valuable documents or photos,  Guaderrama suggests putting them in the freezer (if it’s working) until the house dries out. Strangely enough, the freezer is a low-humidity environment.

Run fans and dehumidifiers and, if it isn’t raining, open doors and windows to get air circulating and dry the space as fast as possible. Hickerson warns that things may look dry when they really aren’t, so he recommends keeping the fans running for at least 48 hours, and perhaps as long as 72 hours.

Once the area is dry, Florida restoration pro Darren Impson advises cleaning and sanitizing with an anti-microbial cleaner. He says you should call a restoration company for this, but it might be hard to schedule one immediately after a disaster.

If you do it yourself, the CDC recommends using dish detergent and water or one cup of bleach per gallon of water. Use bleach only on hard, non-porous surfaces. It doesn’t penetrate porous materials like wood and won’t reach mold embedded in them, so scrub porous surfaces with detergent until the mold is gone.

People often forget to look in HVAC vents, says Hickerson, and if they’re wet enough to support mold, the blower could contaminate the rest of the house as soon as the HVAC system turns on, despite your sanitation efforts.

Uncover any vents that were submerged, ventilate the ducts to dry them out, then sanitize the metal with a bleach solution (metal is non-porous, so bleach is effective). It’s best to wait until you’ve done this before you operate the HVAC system.

#7772. ICE is Now Even More Unpopular than the IRS

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

The agency's growing unpopularity may make it easier to abolish it.

A recent Pew Research Center survey finds that Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is by far the most unpopular federal agency, easily outstripping even the widely despised IRS. According to Pew, 56% of Americans disapprove of ICE, compared to only 35% who approve. That's substantially worse than the IRS (which is disapproved by only a 46-37 margin).

Other recent surveys show growing public support for abolishing ICE. For example, a July YouGov poll indicates that 48% support abolition, compared to 40% who oppose it. Another survey,  conducted in March of this year, showed a similar 50-39 margin in favor of abolition.

The fact that ICE is unpopular doesn't by itself prove the agency should be abolished. Having written a book and many other publications on widespread public ignorance about government policy, I would be the last to argue that popularity is a good metric of a policy's - or an agency's - merit. But, in this case, public opinion is right. As I explained in an August 2025 article in The Hill, and a follow-up piece for the Boston Globe, (non-paywalled version here), ICE's many abuses do indeed justify abolishing it. And the case for doing so has been strengthened by more recent events, such as the brutal killing of two US citizens in Minnesota.

While ICE abuses have been exacerbated by the policies of the second Trump Administration, many predate it, and are inherent in the entire enterprise of mass deportation.

As explained in my article in The Hill, abolishing ICE would not completely end interior deportations. But it would make them heavily dependent on the cooperation of state and local governments, thereby strengthening constitutional federalism and reducing incentives for abuse, at least to a significant degree.

In that article, I also explain how support for abolition be further bolstered by combining it with shifting ICE funds to state and local law enforcement. This undermines the principal political obstacle to abolition: the fear that getting rid of ICE would increase crime. Transferring the funds to state and local police would help defuse such concerns, win the support of law enforcement agencies, and foster genuine reductions in violent and property crimes; social science evidence shows that putting more police on the streets has that effect, whereas deportations do not.

Ilya Somin is Visiting Professor of Law at the University of Virginia, Professor of Law at George Mason University, Simon Chair in Constitutional Studies at the Cato Institute, and author of Free to Move: Foot Voting, Migration, and Political Freedom, Democracy and Political Ignorance: Why Smaller Government is Smarter, and The Grasping Hand: Kelo v. City of New London and the Limits of Eminent Domain.

The Intex Dura-Beam Plus packs a lot of great features into one air mattress. It boasts a built-in electric pump, a valve for a manual pump, a flocked top, a bottom ring for stability, and a raised pillow. It comes in twin and queen sizes, supporting up to 300 pounds and 600 pounds, respectively.

This comfortable mattress from King Koil (which also manufactures traditional mattresses) features an enhanced air coil system to maintain the mattress’s shape and firmness. It also has a few more added luxuries: edge support, a pillow top, a flocked top, and a built-in air pump.

To help guide our decision-making, we reached out to a spokesperson from the American Chiropractic Association for some insight into the best features to look for in an air mattress. Robert Hayden, a chiropractor who owns a practice in Griffin, Georgia, says a selection of firmness levels, as well as self-inflating options, are must-haves. “As you are selecting an air mattress according to your level of comfort, make sure you feel supported in your back, neck, and extremities.”

We kept this advice in mind before testing began, and we researched more than 20 products from eight brands. We scoured product features and user reviews to find the most comfortable, durable, portable, and easiest-to-use inflatable beds for testing. We also wanted to include a group of mattresses that served a variety of budgets, households, and uses. To do that, we looked at products with extra features, such as headboards, cots, and even fun-shaped mattresses for kids.

After extensive research, we landed on 10 beds for our five-person team to test. We assessed comfort, durability, portability, and overall ease of use over 10 days of testing. We inflated and deflated them several times, slept on them, jumped on them, and carried them around our homes. Then we scored each mattress on each of these considerations and awarded them based on their best uses and features. There isn’t a product on this list that we wouldn’t use again.

Whether you’re gearing up for a camping trip or prepping for a visit from the in-laws, an air mattress is a convenient item to have on hand. When choosing the best air mattress for your needs, consider its size, weight limit, materials, and comfort. Also decide if you want any extra comfort and ease-of-use features, like built-in pillows, self-inflating pumps, or “never-flat” options.

Air mattresses are available in common mattress sizes, from toddler to twin to California king. Shoppers will want to consider the best size for their intended use, the number and frequency of house guests, and their available storage space. A twin-size mattress may be suitable for a quick camping trip while a queen-size mattress may better suit a guest room.

Keep in mind, however, that the actual sleeping surface of an air mattress may vary from the dimensions of the air mattress. Air mattresses sometimes bulge out from the head, foot, and sides, creating longer, wider mattress dimensions, but that extra space is not actually usable for sleeping. Taller users and those who intend to share an air mattress may want to look for one that has sides nearly perpendicular to the top. In this type of design, the mattress dimensions and sleeping surface are nearly the same, so buyers don’t have to guess the size of the sleeping surface.

Mattress thickness is another important feature to consider. Air beds can range from thin 3-inch-thick pads for camping to thick 22-inch mattresses for a guest bedroom. A thinner mattress tends to be more portable, affordable, and quicker to inflate. Thick mattresses offer better cushioning and are easier to get up from, but they often come with a larger price tag and are bulkier and heavier to inflate and store.

Portability is an important feature to consider in an air mattress, especially for travel or outdoor use. Some air mattresses deflate to the size of a water bottle and fit into a small bag, making it simple to take on weekend trips and stow away when finished. Also, shoppers will want to consider weight and how much they’re willing to carry up and down a flight of stairs, on a camping trip, or elsewhere. Air mattresses can weigh anywhere between 5 and 50 pounds.

Even if portability isn’t a priority, packable options are generally more compact and easier to store. Plus, a designated storage bag protects the deflated mattress from coming in contact with any messy or sharp items while in storage.

Air mattresses are commonly made of polyvinyl chloride (PVC) or reinforced urethane plastic or rubber. These durable materials are made to be puncture-resistant to prevent damage from pokes and jabs. A puncture-resistant build is especially important for camping and outdoor use. For these activities, make sure to pick a camping air mattress and not an indoor model. Of course, puncture resistance does not guarantee that a rip or tear won’t happen. For that reason, many air mattress brands also include patches, so users can quickly repair the mattress and continue to sleep on it.

Beyond the mattress material, also consider the mattress surface, both on top and bottom. Flocked air mattresses have a soft, velvety finish on top. This textured surface is more comfortable when bed sheets aren’t close by, like while camping, and can also help keep the best bed sheets on when used at home. Nonslip bottoms can prevent the mattress from sliding around.

The best air mattress options are usually easy to inflate and deflate, although some will take a bit more work than others. Inflation methods include manual pumps, electric pumps, and self-inflating or “never-flat” pumps. An air mattress can include a built-in air pump or require an external pump.

Using a manual hand or foot pump takes the most time and effort, but these mattresses are often cost-friendly. They’re also an excellent choice for camping when users might not have a power source. Electric pumps can inflate a mattress in a matter of minutes but will need a power source, like batteries or an AC outlet.

A relatively recent innovation in air mattress design is automatic “smart” or “never-flat” pumps. These pump systems have sensors that monitor the air pressure inside the mattress. If the air pressure drops, the pump will adjust the air pressure as needed to maintain the mattress’s firmness. These smart pumps come at a higher cost but will help a mattress hold firm for a full night’s rest.

A saggy air mattress is uncomfortable at best and can cause back pain at worst. A supportive air mattress maintains an even firmness and does not wobble or sag with every move. A firm mattress top is even more important when sleeping with a partner. When shopping for larger mattresses for two, look for a model with minimal motion transfer.

Quality air mattresses often include features like strategically designed air chambers, vertical air coils, or a firm mattress top to maintain the mattress shape and offer back support. Check out both the inner and edge support. Active sleepers may prefer a mattress with a raised edge so they don’t roll off during the night.

Some air mattress models also include adjustable firmness levels to add to support and comfort. A pillow top or flocked mattress top can offer a soft surface to sleep on.

Hayden also has some expert advice for different sleeping positions on an air mattress. He suggests side sleeping with the use of a body pillow to help take weight off the spine and pelvis. “Adjust the air pressure so that you can sleep on your side comfortably without undue pressure on the shoulder, hip, and knees.”

An air mattress’s weight capacity varies widely depending on its size and design. Weight capacity can range from 200 to 700 pounds.

Since they’re built for one person, single mattresses tend to have a lower weight capacity at around 200 to 300 pounds. Larger mattresses intended for two people will have a higher weight capacity that’s more than 300 pounds. When choosing the ideal weight capacity, it’s best to leave a bit of wiggle room to guarantee that the mattress will offer full support without drooping.

A quality air mattress can include a range of features that add to comfort and ease of use. Extra features can include built-in headboards, USB ports, washable covers, and included sleeping cots.

With a quality air mattress, you’ll always have a comfortable extra bed at a moment’s notice. Since there are so many options, you may have a few lingering questions. Read on for answers to some of the most frequently asked questions about buying and using a new air mattress.

Air mattresses are generally best for short-term use. Most air mattresses won’t provide the consistent support and temperature regulation benefits of a traditional mattress.

While you shouldn’t use an air mattress every day for the reasons mentioned above, we found the EnerPlex air mattress to be extremely comfortable for an air mattress. Its plush, quilted top; cushioned supporting coil beams; and lack of motion transfer made it feel more like a real mattress.

The Coleman Airbed air mattress also makes a great camping option for those who prefer their mattress off the ground, both for comfort and to protect the mattress from damage from an uneven, unpredictable ground surface.

Air mattresses aren’t meant for everyday use, and daily use will cause extra wear and tear on an air mattress, increasing the risk of punctures or stretching. With proper care, a frequently used air mattress can still last a few years. #7770. The Best Fireplace Grates of 2026, Tested and Reviewed

Old Houses AREN’T Scary: What We’ve Learned & Loved About Them

By Mike Larson, Additional research provided by Tony Carrick

Published Oct 28, 2026 9:30 AM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

A good fireplace grate is the unsung hero of any wood-burning hearth. By lifting logs off the floor to improve airflow, it creates a longer, hotter burn while keeping wood safely contained and neatly arranged.

While integral to an efficient fireplace, most grates are surprisingly simple—often just heavy-duty cast iron or steel bars welded together. Still, choosing a well-built model matters. Whether you opt for a steel grate, a cast iron option, or a compact insert for a wood stove, a quality fireplace grate can easily last for decades.

To find the best options, we tested a lineup of popular grates in real fireplaces. The Amagabeli Wrought-Iron Fireplace Log Grate earned our top spot thanks to its heavy-duty build, ample clearance, and angled bars that keep logs in place. Read on for our full reviews of the best fireplace grates available today.

Bottom line: Choosing the right fireplace grate enhances burn efficiency and safety. Our top picks cater to various needs and budgets, ensuring a warm and cozy hearth.

Our list includes fireplace grates that are maneuverable, durable, and thoughtfully designed. These models suit a broad range of fireplace sizes to make any fireplace ready for chilly months.

Our Ratings: Construction 5/5; Efficiency 5/5; Overall Look 5/5; Price 4/5

With a simple design and a durable wrought-iron construction, this V-shaped grate from Amagabeli has six solid steel bars and is a good choice for a grate for a fireplace. Weighing a little more than 20 pounds, the grate that we tested measures 24 inches long by 12.5 inches wide by 7.5 inches high, making it fit most hearths. It also comes in 17-inch and 30-inch options for smaller or larger fireplaces. The angled bars prevent the logs from rolling off, directing them instead toward the center of the grate to feed the fire. The grate’s 4-inch legs provide plenty of air circulation to promote a good burn. An enamel coating on this Amagabeli fireplace grate protects the bars from corrosion, making it suitable for outdoor use, too.

We tested this grate in a number of ways. After building and lighting the fire, we observed how long the fire burned, how much the burning logs moved (if at all), and how the grate looked after the fire. The Amagabeli grate performed excellently, both in terms of how long it kept the fire burning and how little the logs moved while the fire burned. And after the fire died down and we wiped down the soot a little, the enamel on the grate also looked great.

What our tester says: “I loved the look and how easy it was to load the Amagabeli Fireplace grate. For being so simple, I was surprised how efficient it was at keeping the fire burning.”—Mike Larson, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the Amagabeli wrought-iron fireplace grate at Amazon.

Our Ratings: Construction 4/5; Efficiency 4/5; Overall Look 4/5; Price 4/5

Considering its low price, the Pleasant Hearth fireplace grate is one of the better buys we found. However, it does have its drawbacks.The Pleasant Hearth grate has a thinner construction than others we tested, using .5-inch bars instead of larger .75-inch bars, and the difference in the overall look is noticeable. However, the smaller bars do make for a lighter, more easily transportable final product. It’s a nice choice for a small fireplace grate.

The Pleasant Hearth grate holds wood well and keeps a hot fire. We did notice some log movement during our testing; While none of the logs fell completely off of the grate, there was some movement. If logs were piled too high or were unstable, there could potentially be a problem. Another drawback was the ember retainer at the bottom. This device successfully retained coals and prevented them from falling to the hearth floor, but this inadvertently choked the airflow, causing the fire to burn out faster than it might have otherwise. Despite these issues, the Pleasant Hearth grate is a really solid choice for the money.

Get the Pleasant Hearth fireplace grate at Amazon.

Our Ratings: Construction 5/5; Efficiency 5/5; Overall Look 5/5; Price 3/5

Offering a different take on the fireplace grate, this vertical fireplace grate from Grate Wall of Fire features the unique design of most self-feeding fireplace grates. The grate fits at the back of the hearth and pins a stack of logs between it and the fireplace’s back wall, making it an ideal firewood grate. This configuration forces the logs at the top of the stack to fall into the flames as the logs at the bottom burn and crumble.

Because of this setup, we discovered when testing that we could fit a lot more wood in a fire with this grate than any other. Because of its ability to hold the most fuel, the Grate Wall had the longest burning time of any other grate we tested. Overall, this is a very heavy-duty fireplace grate.

In addition to eliminating the need for any tending, this vertical fireplace configuration burns more efficiently, creating more heat and leaving fewer unburned pieces. Since the grate forces that logs to be positioned at the back of wood-burning fireplaces, there’s less opportunity for smoke to escape into the room. It can also act as a fireplace rack for wood. This vertical fireplace grate doesn’t resemble a standard fireplace grate, so those who prefer a classic fireplace look may not like it. Another downside is the price.

What our tester says: “Though this grate is expensive, its high-quality construction means that a customer would likely only ever have to buy it once. Still, it’s pricey for sure.”—Mike Larson, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the Grate Wall of Fire fireplace grate at Amazon.

We got to test a few of the best fireplace grates, but there are several others on the market that might meet your needs. Here are a few others that we’ve come across that have the components we expect to find in quality products, and based on their great reviews, we hope to test them ourselves someday.

Whether it’s Christmas, a chilly night, or a time of celebration, this SteelFreak fireplace grate is a great choice for anyone looking to burn wood in a hearth. Measuring 36 inches in length, this heavy-duty all-steel grate is extra wide and can hold several longer fireplace logs, providing maximum capacity inside a fireplace or a larger fire.

Made in the United States, this SteelFreak fireplace grate is constructed with locally sourced materials and has a tempered design to avoid warping and wear and tear over time. Plus, the .375-inch-thick bars provide added durability, providing owners a lifelong fireplace grate for open wood-burning fireplaces.

Get the SteelFreak fireplace grate at Lowe’s or SteelFreak.

Steel bars with a hexagonal design and large size make this fireplace grate from InnFinest work well for outdoor fireplaces. It consists of eight 0.75-inch-thick bars in a V formation to prevent logs and debris from falling out of the grates. At 23 inches long by 15 inches wide, it can support a large load of logs, such as those typically found in an outdoor fireplace.

Each of these durable grate’s angled bars ensures the wood stays in the fireplace while also helping to keep the fire going by directing logs toward the center. A little more than 8.5 inches tall, it has plenty of airflow to promote a good burn. Plus, this model comes fully assembled and ready to use.

Get the InnFinest fireplace grate at Amazon.

We considered several factors when choosing the best fireplace grates, including quality of construction, design, weight, and size. We chose only grates constructed from a single piece of forged iron or steel. With regard to design, we featured grates with at least 3 inches of clearance from the hearth floor to ensure ample airflow. We also favored grates with curved tines that secured the logs while also helping feed them to the flames.

We tested the grates by building fires on them and burning. After we loaded them to capacity with logs and lit them, we timed how long it was until the fire burned out completely. We also used a high-temperature digital thermometer to test how hot the fires burned. Our final test included doing a visual inspection of the grate after the fire burned and the grate had cooled.

Before buying a fireplace grate, shoppers will want to understand the difference between each type and learn how size, shape, and material affect performance. All of these factors play an important role in selecting the best fireplace grate for a home. Here is a closer look at all of these factors and features along with other important characteristics to help shoppers find the right fireplace grates.

There are three types of fireplace grates: bar, basket, and vertical. Bar varieties have parallel steel bars that are welded to four legs and elevate the logs a few inches off of the hearth. Basket fireplace grates are typically made from a single piece of cast iron. While they’re typically more expensive, they can also hold much more wood securely. Vertical fireplace grates hold a bundle of logs in a 90-degree angle, pinning them against the rear of the hearth and dropping a fresh one down onto the embers as older ones burn, limiting the amount of smoke that can escape.

A fireplace grate must fit inside the firebox of the fireplace. While a grate that’s too large won’t fit, a grate that’s too small won’t be able to hold enough logs to maximize the fireplace’s potential.

Fireboxes don’t come in standard sizes, so measure the firebox of a fireplace and pay attention to the dimensions of the grate when shopping. You’ll want to measure the height, width, and depth of the firebox to ensure a proper fit.

You should also measure the width in both the front and the back, as fireplaces typically taper from the front of the firebox to the back. A fireplace log grate shouldn’t fit in the box like a glove; instead, it needs about 3 inches of clearance between it and the fireplace on all sides.

Most fireplace grates have bars that curve upward on the front and back. This curved design is intentional, and it serves two purposes: It prevents logs from rolling off while also directing unburned ones toward the embers in the middle of the grate. As the logs burn in the fireplace, gravity guides them to the middle of the hearth, helping them burn more efficiently without the need to push the logs back into place with a poker. Most fireplace grates also taper from the front to the back to match the typical shape of a hearth for a better fit.

Steel and cast-iron grates are suitable options for a fireplace. Cast-iron grates are typically made from one solid piece of metal. By contrast, steel-bar grates are usually made from multiple pieces of extruded square tubes that are welded together.

Because of their single-piece construction, cast-iron grates are more durable than steel varieties, and they have excellent heat-retention properties. Cast-iron fireplace grates are also considerably heavier and more expensive than steel fireplace grates. Steel fireplace grates are cheaper but won’t last as long. Some models have an enamel coating that makes them suitable for use in outdoor fireplaces and fire pits.

Structurally, fireplace grates consist of bars that cradle the logs and legs that support the bars, elevating them off the base of the hearth. Most grates consist of six or seven bars. The more bars, the more securely the fireplace grate can support the wood. These bars are typically curved to keep logs at the center of the grate while also preventing them from shifting and rolling out of the hearth. Most fireplace grates have four legs to support the bars. The legs elevate the logs about 3 to 4 inches off the floor of the hearth, allowing for ventilation, which promotes a good burn.

Some fireplace grates have a steel mesh or grille-like bottom. This feature prevents small pieces of burning wood from falling through the grate and landing on the hearth. Because the mesh catches much of the ash the fire produces, it makes the fireplace grate much easier to clean.

Fireplace grates that have a mesh bottom help keep a fire together, promoting a more robust, hotter burn. How the mesh is patterned typically depends on the metal used (typically steel or cast-iron varieties) to make the fireplace grate and whether the grate itself will be used to burn coal or wood.

A fireplace grate for a wood-burning fireplace offers several advantages. Airflow is key to achieving a good burn in a wood-burning fireplace. Grates facilitate airflow by raising the wood off the hearth by 3 to 4 inches, allowing oxygen to circulate below the logs.

Designed to endure for many years, lifetime fireplace grates reduce the amount of tending needed to keep the fire burning while also making it safer. The curved tines of a grate push the logs toward the burning embers, so the user doesn’t have to do it manually. The bars also help contain shifting logs, reducing the risk that a burning log can roll into the room.

A fireplace log grate isn’t simply about improving the aesthetics and performance of a fireplace; it’s also about safety. Fireplace grates help keep the logs and the fire contained, reducing the chances that an ember or burning log can escape the firebox. A fireplace grate should fit the firebox well and have about 3 inches of buffer on all sides.

Fireplace grates must be moved periodically to sweep up the ash that accumulates underneath. Shoppers should purchase a grate that’s light enough to lift and maneuver in and out of the hearth’s firebox.

To load a fireplace grate properly, place two timbers on the grate followed by tinder and kindling. Additional logs can then be placed on top of the tinder and kindling. A fireplace grate should never be overloaded, as too much wood could cause logs to roll off and into the room.

Here are answers to the most common questions about fireplace grates.

Cast-iron fireplace grates are the best metal for a fireplace grate. These grates eliminate the need for welds that can potentially fail and also retain heat better than steel.

Fireplace grates are measured in length and depth. A fireplace grate usually needs about 3 inches of free space around all sides to promote proper airflow.

To clean a fireplace grate, remove any ash or soot buildup with a dry rag. Water should not be used because it can cause rust.

Yes, a wood-burning fireplace can be used without a grate. A grate simply allows a fire to burn more efficiently while making it easier to manage.

While there is no set height, a good fireplace grate will have at least 3 inches of clearance beneath it to allow for maximum airflow. A grate that’s highest point is at least 10 inches off the ground will keep wood held in tight.

For safety and the best burning fire, wood should be stacked uniformly, running lengthwise down the grate.

Larger grates can hold more wood, and as such, they’ll produce longer-burning fires. However, the most important reason to consider size is to be sure the grate fits properly into your fireplace or fire pit; if it’s too small, the fireplace won’t be maximized in terms of the heat it can produce or the ambiance, but if the frate is too large it will burn inefficiently or be dangerous.
